PERSONAL EXPLANATION-HON. WM. ROSS-DENNIS EAGAN LETTER.
speechtext:
I would ask the indulgence of the House while I make a personal explanation in connection with the charge that was made against me by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain). The hon. member read from the Journals of the House and he had my denial before him when he made the charge. I am not going to read the whole of that denial. I said that I was in a position to give the

strongest and most emphatic denial the English language would enable me to do. I shall not, however, trouble the House with the whole of my personal denial which I made thirty years ago in this House. The hon. gentleman had my denial before him on the same page from which he read and we know what is thought of the man who conceals the truth. The same charge was made against me in a Tory paper in the year 1878 in the island of Cape Breton and 1 replied to it, also in a Conservative paper, as follows :
X did not think that out of some self respect, the old infamous charge that I wrote the * Dennis Eagan letter ' would be repeated, particularly as the most learned of the proprietors of the ' Advocate ' stated, ' we know now that Mr. Ross did not write the Dennis Eagan letter.' A more dishonest and disgraceful accusation was never made by one man against another. I stated in my place in parliament, as I now repeat in the strongest and most emphatic language, that it is possible for me to use, that I never by pen, pencil, or by any act of mine wrote the said letter, and that I never saw it. I was promised that it should be placed in my hands, hut that written promise was never fulfilled, but thinking it would, I had copies of it lithographed in pencil and ink as if written by me, so that they could be compared with the original, and I now send you the said copies and ask the editor of the ' Advocate ' if he has any regard for honest and truthful inquiry to compare it with the real letter which he still unjustly repeats was written by me. Why was this letter never produced in parliament and shown to those who are familiar with my writing ? In Victoria Dominion officials wandered about canvassing against me, and though asked, I never would so far forget my position as to write or use anything against them, and it would be folly to imagine that I would have followed any other course in Cape Breton. When the statement was made in parliament that I wrote the said letter, I telegraphed to North Sydney for information, and received the following reply from John Vooght, Esq. : ' You are at liberty to state in your place in parliament that I can prove that you did not write the Dennis Eagan letter.' I therefore, hurl back this vile slander, to the source from which it emanated, as the most unfounded and false accusation that it was possible to be made against me. If the editor of the ' Advocate ' could be moved to that sense of honour that should characterize noble minded men, instead of reiterating this slander, he will express his regret that he was entrapped and seduced to write what he must now know, was pure and unfounded.
The editor of the paper, also then a warm Conservative, wrote the following :
In the spirit of fair-play that has always characterized our paper, we have published Hon. William Ross's letter knowing that many of his friends in Victoria are our friends and subscribers. It is also due to Mr. Ross that we state that we have full and ample proof that the ' Dennis Eagan ' letter, of which such public use was made, was not written by him. A regard for truth and justice compels us to make this fact known to Mr. ROSS (Victoria).
our readers, were it necessary we could here write the name of the author of said letter, having the pleasure of seeing him almost every day. Nothing can indeed be gained by this unfair abuse of one who has retired from public life, and who has left a record behind him in Victoria and Cape Breton, for honour, justice, and Integrity In all his public career, which it would be well that others of greater sound and pretensions would follow and imitate.
Sir Charles Tupper made the same charge against me, and I Wrote him giving an explanation. Sir Charles Tupper, acting as a man of honour and a gentleman, made this public announcement, which will be found on page 1077 of the ' Hansard ' of 1887 :
I wish to make a very brief statement to the House before the orders of the day are called. The House will remember that, on a recent occasion, when the question arose of the policy of various governments in regard to the action of subordinate officers, I read a letter to the House which was handed to me by an hon. member who sits behind me, from a printed paper published at the time, which was some time ago, and which I had no idea was not authentic. It purports to be a letter written by Mr. Wm. Ross, then a member of this House, and at one time a member of the government ; and when I read that letter to the House I had entirely forgotten when it was originally produced, its authenticity was challenged. That statement was made by an hon. gentleman opposite, and I think it is right that I should say that I have received a letter from Mr. Ross calling my attention to the fact of his having denied the authenticity of the letter, and assuring me that the letter was a forgery. I take this opportunity of stating to the House that I accept that statement. I have not the slightest doubt of the accuracy of the statement made by this gentleman, who at this moment holds a very high and important office under the government. I have very great pleasure in making the fullest amend to the hon. gentleman, and in expressing my regret that I should have forgotten, what I now remember, that at the time the letter was produced, its authenticity was denied.
There is the statement of a gentleman. When I placed the matter before him, he gave a public denial of the charge he had read. I think that that is an example which should be followed by men who would like to be called gentlemen in this House, and who should regret having brought a false accusation against another hon. member. This false accusation was publicly denied by me thirty years ago and my denial was accepted, but to-day we find an hon. gentleman who would stoop to revive this old calumny. A more disgraceful accusation was never made in this House by one member against an other. It was due to myself and my constituency, to my friends in Halifax and in this House-and I have friends on both sides ; so much so that gentlemen on the other side express to me their regret that this old disproved accusation should have been revived-it is due to all parties. I say' that I should take this occasion to again

show up the falsity of this charge, and I trust we will hear no more of it.

speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) will appreciate the reason of the ruling that a member can speak only once on the same question. If he were allowed to move amendment after amendment there would be no end to some debates.
I understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I quite agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) who has said that there is no good purpose to be served by prolonged discussion of these amendments as they come up. They were fully discussed last year when they were up in this House, and this session in the Railway Committee, to say nothing about the discussion in the committee of this House. So far as this particular amendment is concerned, I do not see why I should depart from the opinion I expressed before, when I said that it seemed to me there were doubts as to whether we had the power to deal with this amendment. My hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) will remember that when the question was up on a former occasion, the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) concurred with me in the opinion that there were these doubts. I believe that if we adopted this amendment, the Railway Act would have to be recast in many particulars to make it workable.
Would the House object, Mr. Speaker, to the name of my hon. friend from Peel, (Mr. Blain) being substituted for mine as the mover of this amendment ?
The amendment is in the hands of the House and the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Maclean's) name cannot be withdrawn except by unanimous consent.

As my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) was under a slight misapprehension as to the rules of the House, I think this concession ought to be made to him without question. Before the amendment is put, I desire to say that I agree absolutely with the view expressed by my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) that it is proper that express companies should be

controlled. The subject was discussed last year when the Hailway Act went through. The express business, however, it must be noticed, is somewhat different from the ordinary railway business. The goods sent by express are collected sometimes from street to street or from house to house. The work involves cartage, and it also involves arrangements with steamship lines, stage lines and so on. It is a more complicated subject, so far as dealing with the rates is concerned, than the control over railway rates exercised by the Railway Commission. I have looked carefully over the Railway Act and I find that there is no provision of special importance with regard to express companies except section 278 which reads as follows :
Every company which grants any facilities for the carriage of goods by express to any incorporated express company or person, shall grant equal facilities, on equal terms and conditions, to any other incorporated express company which demands the same.
That is designed, I suppose, for the purpose of preventing a monopoly by any company of the express business over any particular railway. It has been said in this House that that section has not fulfilled the purpose for which Jt was designed. I have been referred to litigation which was instituted for the purpose of enforcing the provisions of this section before the present Railway Commission was established. So far as my opinion is concerned, I should think that that section is capable of being enforced. Our commission has power of enforcement of that section differing somewhat from the powers of similar tribunals in the United States of America. Of course, it would be some relief to establish competition, if competition be possible. I have heard it stated by those who have studied the matter somewhat that it is not very easy, upon a single line of railway to have competing express companies. If that be so, and if, as a matter of practice, the purpose of section 278 cannot be carried out, that affords all the more reason why there should be in Canada some effective control of the rates charged by express companies. I believe that the express rates in this country, in many departments of business at least, have been very materially reduced within the last eight or ten years. I have been so informed by those who are in a position to know, and I believe the statement is correct. The express companies are doing a very large and very important work. I was surprised, on making some investigations into the question to learn how large the amount of traffic carried by the express companies has become. But that is a further reason why there should be control of rates. On looking over the statute. I concur in the view expressed by the Minister of Justice that to merely insert the words ' express companies ' as proposed by the amendment of my hon. friend, Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
would not only result in uncertainty and confusion, but would probably render the Act absolutely ineffective so far as any attempt to control the express companies is concerned. Therefore, my position with regard to the matter is this : I believe in the control of rates of the express companies. I recognize the fact that control must come, and that it ought to come at the earliest possible date, but I do not believe that it can be attained by the insertion of two words in this Bill. While I sympathize with the motive of my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) and am absolutely in favour of some control being exercised upon the rates of express companies, I do not think that purpose can be effected in this way. I will be prepared, however, to support a bill with proper conditions, which, I hope, will be brought in for the purpose of exercising over the rates of express companies a control similar to that which at present is exercised by the board of railway commissioners upon the rates of railway companies. It is for that reason, and that alone, that I could not support the amendment of my hon. friend. I think it will be ineffective and will only end in confusion. At the same time, as I say, I absolutely sympathize with the motive which actuates him in proposing this amendment and 1 will be prepared to carry it into effect in the proper way.

I am heartily in sympathy with the proposal to put express companies under the control of the Railway Commission. I do not see why an off-shoot from the railway companies such as express companies, doing a business probably, of $2,000,000, as near as I can find out from the report of the Minister of Railways, should not come under the control of the Raijway Commissioners. But, while I am heartily in sympathy with this idea, the matter has come up in such a way that it seems impossible for us, if we are well advised by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick), and the leader pf the opposition (Mr. R- L- Borden) to vote for the motion nowr standing in the name of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain). I shall have to vote against it, considering that I am legally advised that it will be of no use. But my opinion is not changed. I am still heartily in favour of the control of express companies by the Railway Commission, and I hope that the government at an early day will bring in a measure to effect that change.

As my name has been substituted for that of the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) as mover of this amendment. I wish to say a few words. AVhen this question was before the Committee of the AVhole House a few days ago. I expressed myself as in accord with the principle of the amendment. I have not since changed my opinion ; I am still in favour

of the motion that I propose to ask the House to vote upon. I am of opinion that the people of this country believe that the express companies should be controlled by the Railway Commission as the freight rates of railways are controlled by this eommis-. Sion. Hon. members, of course, are aware that a considerable proportion of the goods now consumed by the Canadian people, especially in the older provinces, are carried by express. In the central part of the province of Ontario the farmers are devoting themselves to the cultivation * of such products as must find their way to the market in large centres by means of express carriage. The farmers in the immediate vicinities of the larger cities are almost compelled, these times, to send their products by express to the consumers. Indeed there are many farmers in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec the larger portion of whose products are carried by express to market. The House must remember that the farmers are particularly interested in this matter ; and while it has been said by ,the Minister of Justice that possibly this motion will not cover all that is required, and will not place the express companies under the control of the Railway Commission, yet the House must bear in mind that the government had distinct notice of this proposition one year ago. One year ago my hon. friend from East York brought this matter before the House, and called the attention of the Minister of Railways to the fact that it was desired that the express companies should come under the operation of the Railway Commission. I am of the opinion that the government since last year has had ample notice, and I think the people of Canada will consider it to be the duty of the government at this session of parliament to introduce such legislation as will place the express companies under the control of the Railway Commission. I shall support this amendment. If it does not measure up to the requirements of the people on this question, then I think it is the duty of the government, who have power to legislate, to substitute for this amendment, if the House so expresses its will, such legislation at this session as will bring the express companies under the control of the Railway Commission.

The division that has just taken place is rather portentous.' It may mean a new era in this country and it. shows that at the present time the people are beginning to see where they are in regard to this new and progressive question. I now beg to move the following amendment :

Sec.-Treas.
I have a similar letter from the Farmers' Association of the county of Haldimand, Mr. MACLEAN.
from Algoma, from South Huron, from West Simcoe-all these name their members and trust they will support the motion ; from East Kent, from North Wentworth, from East Lambton, from South Wellington, from Lennox, another from Kent, from the Ratepayers' Association of Toronto and a number of others. They are all to this effect, that parliament is the only body that can regulate a standard passenger rate, that it ought to be defined, that it is in the interest of the public that it should be defined, and that wherever a passenger rate has been defined by parliament or by a legislature lower passenger rates have resulted. Notwithstanding all that has been said in this House about the smallness of the law in Michigan and about the smallness of the law in the state of New York, the great fact is that the majority of the travel-again I assert it in this House without fear of contradiction- the majority of the travel in the state of New York and the majority of the travel in the state of Michigan by reason of the legislation there, is for 2 cents, and less than 2 cents. 1 say this, that in a number of states where they have advertised a thousand mile' ticket for $20, which is 2 cents a mile, good results have come from it, and that the time has arrived when we must have a standard passenger rate fixed in this country. I assume to fix it by this amendment, and fix it as fairly as can be under the circumstances.

Before the motion is put I desire to offer a few observations in regard to it. I thought that my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) was going to speak. I yield to no one in appreciating the importance of reasonable passenger rates in this country but I think it is undesirable that we should pass any legislation which might result in the postponement for an indefinite period of what we would regard as reasonable passenger rates. The motion of my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) provides that :
The tolls charged in any standard passenger tariff shall not exceed the following, namely :-for all companies the gross earnings of whose passenger trains, as reported to the Minister of Railways, under the provisions of section 304 of this Act, equalled or exceeded the sum of $3,000 for each mile of road operated by the said company, two (2) cents per mile ; and for all companies, the earnings of whose passenger trains, reported as aforesaid, were over $2,000 and less than $3,000 per mile of the road operated by the said company, two and one-half (21) cents per mile ; and for all companies whose earnings, reported as aforesaid, were less than $2,000 per mile of road operated by the said company, three (3) cents per mile.
The basis of that legislation, as I understand it, is to be found in certain legislation of the state of Michigan which legislation, I am informed, does not apply to the whole state of Michigan. It applies to only

a portion of the state of Michigan. In order that we should go to the state of Michigan for the purpose of establishing the basis of our railway legislation in Canada we must first be absolutely certain that the conditions in the state of Michigan and in Canada are precisely the same. I have not heard up to the present time anything which would convince me of that. The state of Michigan contains a little less'than 7,000 miles of railway, while the Dominion of Canada, I suppose thirty times as large, contains something less than 19,000 miles of railway. The state of Michigan is populated very much more densely than the Dominion of Canada as a whole. Unless I am convinced by a better argument than that which I have heard that the conditions in the state of Michigan are exactly the same as they are in Canada, and I do not believe they are, I do not propose to go to the state of Michigan to find out what sort of legislation we should pass in regard to this subject. If we pass this statute the Railway Commission of Canada will properly consider it binding upon them and for that reason they will for all time to come govern themselves by it and thus they will be unable to give us a two-cent rate in many parts of the country where the conditions provided for by this amendment do not prevail and for many years are not likely to exist. It seems to me much more probable that this amendment will retard the establishment of reasonable railway rates in this country, as a whole, than that it will improve our opportunities in that regard.
I do not know whether those who promote this legislation have investigated all the conditions in the state of Michigan. Has any hon. member of this House, for example, investigated the remuneration of railways in Canada as compared with the remuneration of railways in the state of Michigan for the carriage of the mails ? I suppose that is a fairly important subject to consider. In the state of Michigan with less than 7,000 miles of railway more than $1,000,000 are paid every year for the carriage of the mails. In the Dominion of Canada with railways extending over an enormous area and totalling 19,000 miles, we pay only $400,000 more for the carriage of the mails, namely, $1,413,835. These are matters which are proper to be considered before we undertake to apply the Michigan legislation to the Dominion of Canada.
But, the most important objection I have to this amendment is that within six months after we have appointed a tribunal for the purpose of dealing with this very subject and before we have had the slightest experience of the public benefit which would result from the work of that tribunal we propose to take out of the hands of the tribunal the very work that parliament has entrusted to it.

Yes. I do not think that is good legislation. I should thiuk that parliament, after having committed this whole subject, to the Railway Commission by legislation, after having conferred upon that commission as large powers as were ever conferred on any similar body, should, within six months and before any opportunity has been given to ascertain the benefits to be derived from the commission, proceed to take from that commission the very work which was entrusted to it. If we propose to deal with passenger rates why not deal with freight rates in this way ? Freight rates are more important to the people of this country than passenger rates. Any farmer in this country who spends $20 in the course of the year in passenger rates will perhaps pay $200 in freight rates so that the all important question is rather freight rates than passenger rates. Besides, as has been pointed out in this House and I think in the committee, passenger rates are to a large extent ameliorated by the fact that we have excursions from time to time, cheap rates, which are taken advantage of by the people of the country, whereas there are no cheap excursion freight rates in this country. I think that if parliament were to proceed to deal with this question of passenger rates in this way it would be stultifying itself unless it proceeded at the same time to abolish the whole Railway Commission and to deal also with the subject of freight rates. If this motion means anything it means that the legislation which we passed last year was of no avail.
Now, what effect would this legislation have if applied in Canada at the present time ? The Canadian Northern Railway has earnings of $315 per mile. How long will it be before we get a passenger rate of two cents on the Canadian Northern ? The earnings of that railway must increase from $315 per mile to $3,000 per mile before we shall get a two-cent rate on the Canadian Northern.
We have a three-cent rate on it now by the legislation of last year.

The object is to get a two-cent rate upon it and this legislation will produce a two-cent rate on the Canadian Northern when the passenger earnings have increased ten times what they are at the present time.
I grant you that ; but it will get you a two-cent passenger rate on the Grand Trunk Railway to-morrow.

The Canada Atlantic Railway earns $670 per mile. We will get a two-cent rate on the Canada Atlantic when its earnings have increased to five times what they are at present. That does not seem to promise any very early relief on that railway. The Canadian Pacific Rail-

way earns SI.400 per mile. We will get a two-cent rate by tliis legislation wlien tlie passenger earnings of the Canadian Pacific Railway have something more than doubled. Is that very likely to occur within the next ten years ? It does not seem to me that the legislation suggested by my hon. friend, and I appreciate and sympathize with the motives which have led him to propose it, is likely to result in a very great amelioration of passenger rates in the early future.
What about the Grand Trunk ?
The Grand Trunk earns $2,200 per mile and under that the Grand Trunk would be entitled to charge two and a half cents per mile.
To-morrow.
To-morrow, and we have legislation at the present time on the statute-book which obliges the Grand Trunk to charge only two cents per mile and I have heard my hon. friend argue that in- this House.
For third-class passengers.

Well, for third-class passengers, but inasmuch as third-class passenger traffic is abolished in this country, and that practically there is very little distinction between first-class and second-class, it would not seem that the legislation existing on the statute-book has had very much influence upon the Grand Trunk.
I can see what this legislation would result in if applied to a great railway system like the Grand Trunk. It would simply result in the Grand Trunk Railway putting under separate corporations a number of branches which are now included in its general system and it would impose on the people in remote and sparsely settled portions of the country a higher railway tariff than they are subjected to at the present time. That seems to be the propable result. At the present time you have a great system. you have eight or ten or twelve roads which were formerly operated by eight or ten or twelve companies, operated by one company, and under the management of one company-the Grand Trunk Railway system. But if legislation of this kind were put on the statute-books, the Grand Trunk Railway would naturally retain under the management of the parent company only those main lines whose earnings would bring them under the terms of this statute, and it no doubt would seek to place under separate corporate management the subsidiary companies running through sparsely settled portions of the country, because the earnings on these portions of the road would not come within the operation of this statute. It seems to me that this would be the result of legislation of this kind. Thus sparsely Mr. R. L. BORDER.
settled districts would pay higher railway rates.
But why should we seek in this parliament to deal with this matter in this way when we have in the Railway Commission of Canada the most ample powers that any tribunal ever possessed for dealing with it. Let us look at some of those powers and inquire if there is any reason why we should pass by the Railway Commission. Let me say that the Railway Commission of Canada differs in important respects from many similar tribunals. I supported the idea of a Railway Commission before a measure for its creation was ever submitted to parliament:; I supported it for what I thought were good reasons. The Act we have passed confers on the Railway Commission power not only to fix rates, but to enforce them, and in that very important respect it differs from the Interstate Commerce Commission, and from other tribunals in the United States, very few of which have any power of enforcement. For instance, the question of rates is fought out before the Interstate Commerce Commission, but you have to go to the courts to enforce the decision and there the decision of the Interstate Commission is found not to be binding. A railway corporation is able to fight out the whole question again in the courts, and it is only by obtaining the judgment of the courts that eventually you obtain a declaration against the rates disallowed by the Interstate Commerce Commission. In section 251 of our Railway Act there is this provision :
The company may from time to time prepare and issue tariffs of the tolls to be charged as hereinafter provided, for all traffic carried by the company upon the railway.
The word ' traffic ' includes passengers as well as freight.
Section 251, clause 2 says :
All such by-laws shall be submitted to and approved by the board.
' These tariffs can thus have no effect whatever until approved of by the board. Section 252 says :
Such tolls may be either for the whole or for any particular portions of the railway ; but all such tolls shall always under substantially similar circumstances and conditions be charged equally to all persons, and at the same rate.
Section 252, subsection 3 says :
No tolls shall be charged which unjustly discriminate between different localities.
Section 257 says :
The board may disallow any tariff, or any portion thereof which it considers to be unjust or unreasonable, or contrary to any of the provisions of this Act, and may require the company, within a prescribed time, to substitute a tariff satisfactory to the board in Peu then of, or may prescribe other tolls in lie i of the tolls so disallowed, and may designate the date at which any tariff shall come into force.

Section 263 says :
The tariff of tolls which tlie company shall be authorized to issue under this Act for the carriage of passengers between points on the railway shall be divided into two cases, namely :
The maximum mileage tariff, herein referred to as standard passenger tariff ;
An 1 reduced passenger tariffs, herein referred to as special passenger tariffs.
2.	The standard passenger tariff shall specify the maximum mileage tolls to be charged for passengers for all distances covered by the company's railway ; such distances may be expressed in like manner as provided herein in respect of standard freight tariffs.
3.	Special passenger tariffs shall specify the toll or tolls to be charged by the company for passengers in every case where such tolls are lower than the tolls specified in the company's standard passenger tariff.
Section 264 says :
A standard passenger tariff shall be filed, approved and published in the same manner as required by this Act in the case of a freight standard tariff.
Section 265 says :
All special passenger tariffs shall be filed by the company with the board, and published as required by section 274, three days before any such tariff is intended to take effect.
Section 274 provides that the company shall at each station deposit and keep on file at a convenient place for the inspection of the public its standard and special passenger tariffs and freight tariffs of both classes. It shall also, in some public place in its stations give notice as to where Its tariffs can be inspected.
Therefore you have under this statute complete and ample provisions for dealing not only with freight rates, but with passenger rates. You have a commission appointed for that purpose. You have a commission which has powers of investigation which are not possessed by this parliament, and I cannot at the present time see any good reason why that duty which parliament in its wisdom has committed to the Railway Commission only last year, should be taken away from it, and that we should proceed to deal with a subject which certainly we cannot investigate as fully or as carefully as can that tribunal. If we are to accept this amendment, then it seems to me that it was very unwise to undertake an annual expenditure of $100,000 or $150,000 for the purpose of maintaining this commission. We have thought it wise to entrust to the commission these duties, and if now we are able to take them upon ourselves, this expenditure of public money would be useless. I say that if you pass legislation such as is suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) it would in the first place give the railway companies an opportunity of demanding higher rates on freight; in the second place it would give them an excuse for abolishing all excursion rates, and it might eventually
result in a poorer service in districts where there is no competition. Moreover, it adopts the principle that rates shall be graded according to earnings, and therefore it must result in higher rates for sparsely settled districts where the earnings are smaller. Further, it might cause them to carry on their branch lines under separate corporate entities, so as to avoid bringing these branch lines under the terms of the proposed, statute.
I believe in giving the railway commission an opportunity to demonstrate its usefulness. If it does not justify its existence by establishing reasonable passenger and freight rates in this country, it is because the personnel of the commission is not suitable, or because the powers which have been conferred upon it are not sufficient. I am prepared to support the administration in dealing with either of these defects should they become apparent. I do not understand that any such difficulty has arisen up to this time. Let us therefore give the Railway Commission an opportunity to know what it can do, and if from either of these causes, of which I have spoken, it does not do the necessary work, then let us reorganize the commission or amend the legislation.
in conclusion, it seems to me that the legislation to which my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) has directed the attention of the House might eventually result in comparatively low fares in thickly settled portions of the country, and in much higher fai'es in x'emote districts. That would be the natural tendency, if the principle of this legislation were insisted upon. In saying what I do, I trust I do not fail to appreciate the efforts which my hon. friend from Bast York (Mr. Maclean) is making in the public interest. I sympathize in the objects which he has in view. The only difference between us is. that I think, considering the legislation of last year, his objects can be best accomplished by the Railway Commission which we have appointed for that purpose. He thinks on the contrary, that it is wise, within certain limitations to take that work out of the hands of the Railway Commission and to establish a standard according to earnings, which, in his opinion, would have excellent results, but which does not present itself to me in that view. For these reasons which I have very briefly stated, I cannot support the amendment of my hon. friend from York (Mr. Maclean).

I supported the principle of this amendment some years ago in this House. I have had discussions with the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) regarding it. and I reached an understanding with him as to what principle i would support, and this amendment being in harmony with that principle I believe it my duty to support it. I wish for a few moments to refer to an argument made by the leader of the opposition that it would ! result in higher freight rates. Of course it

might, there is no question about that. If the railroads did not find it paying, they might charge higher freight rates, but I am told, although I am not prepared to vouch for the correctness of the statement, that in Southern Michigan where the law applies, it has not resulted in higher freight rates and therefore, I would assume that that is not likely to happen here.
Then it was said that if this law is passed we might not have excursions. 1 again turn to Michigan for an example. I find that excursions there are as numerous as in Canada and yet, this law applies to the Southern part of Michigan, so I do not think that any fear is to be apprehended from that.
It is also said that it might result in portions of the railway system being put under a different management. I think that is not at all likely to happen. Because this only applies to a company whose passenger earnings reach $3,000 a mile, and in the remote portions of the country this amount would not be reached so that the law could not apply to them and there would be no necessity for putting such a section under a new management.
The next argument was that we should not copy Michigan in this unless everything there is on all fours with the conditions in Canada. We who live in Ontario adjoin the state of Michigan, and are back and forth among Michigan people very frequently and know the state well, always regard Michigan as being the same type of country as Ontario. We do not see much difference when we cross the border between the pursuits of the people and the conditions of life. The railroad operations are much the same and therefore 1 could not see any serious objection to following the example of Michigan.
One objection raised was that this measure applied only to a certain locality. In my judgment this provision was made simply for this reason, that the southern portion of Michigan is thickly settled, while the northern portion is still a comparatively new country and not thickly settled. To make it apply to the northern peninsula, a new section of country, was deemed improper owing to the comparatively light travel on the railways there. But X think it might well be left to apply to the whole country because when the earnings reach $3,000 a mile, it would be regarded as fair that the company should reduce its passenger rate to 2 cents a mile.
A word with regard to the question of whether we should introduce this law in view of the fact that the Railway Act was passed last session. To my mind that is a very strong argument against it, the strongest we have heard advanced, because the clauses of the Act which the leader of the opposition has cited seem to very amply cover the ground, and our Railway Commission has the substantial advantage over the Mr. SPROULE.	.

It does not for instance, apply to government or provincial railways, but only to those under federal control. It may be said that if we * pass such a law here, we could only enforce il upon the railways under our control. I may say, Sir, that in Manitoba, as is very well known to the members of this House, the provincial government have control of the freight and passenger rates of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. They have that control, subject to an arrangement that until the rates are reduced to a certain figure if there should be any loss in the operation of the railway the province is not to bear that loss but when the freight rates come down to, 1 think, 10 cents a hundred, then. If the company should lose on the, operation of the road the province is to bear any such loss. The provincial government have control of the passenger and freight rates and if this measure which is proposed by the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) was to pass

it would take away that control which we believe is essential and which now gives to the province the power of regulating the rates and at the same time protecting the people from having to meet any deficiency. On the other hand if this-resolution was to come into force and any loss should accrue in the operation of the Canadian Northern the people of the province would suffer. As the leader of the opposition (Mr. It. L. Borden) has remarked, the matter of freight rates is of a great deal more importance, so far as the farmers in Manitoba are concerned, than are the passenger rates, because the farmers are not the people who travel a great deal. It is the other people of the country who do the travelling and pay out' the greater portion of the passenger receipts of the railways. But the farmers of Manitoba pay possibly an average of $150 to $200 in freight rates, which is of a great deal more im-Ijortance to them than the question of passenger rates. I think that the same would apply to the whole farming community of Canada. If the farmers would stop to think about it, they would find that the legislation proposed is not in their interests but rather in the interests of the people of the cities and the commercial people.
I have fifty letters here from farmers in favour of it.

The farmers at times are misled, and I do not know any one better qualified sometimes to lead them astray than my hon. friend. I represent a farming community and am always ready to discuss anything with them and prepared to show them why I take any line, and I would be quite prepared to discuss this question with them. I say that the passenger traffic is a great deal more important to the commercial interests, and this resolution would be of greater benefit to the commercial people than to the farming communities. If the hon. gentleman would introduce something which would lower the rates of freight on the 2,000 or 3,000 bushels of wheat which the average farmer raises in Manitoba, he would be doing something more beneficial to them than he could possibly do by this proposition, which I would call ' a catch vote ' if introduced by some people. The Canadian Pacific Railway, I understand, have an average passenger rate to-day under two cents a mile, so that I do not see of what benefit my hon. friend's resolution, if adopted, could be to anybody. As shown by the leader of the opposition, it would not apply to the Canadian Northern, the Canada Atlantic, the Canadian Pacific or the Grand Trunk Railway. What then is the use of it ?

Does the hon. gentleman say it will not apply to the Grand Trunk Railway ? It would give a two and a half cents per mile rate and on the Michigan
Central would give a two-cent rate to-morrow.

I am speaking of the roads I am more familiar with. As far as the people of Canada as a whole are concerned, this would not be of any particular benefit to them. I am in favour of low passenger rates. I believe that if the railway companies would consult their own interests, it might be better for them to charge a lower rate and increase their traffic, but they seem to understand that question and they so regulate their rates that on the Canadian Pacific Railway the average is under two cents a mile. The hon. gentleman's resolution, if adopted, would interfere with the arrangements which the Manitoba government have made with the Canadian Northern and impose a burden on the people of that province which we ought not to do, and I am going to vote against the amendment.

I might explain that this amendment deals with the telephone question. The Bell Telephone Company has made contracts with the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern, whereby independent telephones or municipal telephones are prohibited from entering the railway station. The law was amended last session so as to provide, according to the solemn pledge of the Minister of Railways of that time, that these railway companies should be compelled to give access to their stations to independent telephones on payment of actual damage. The Railway Commission has since held that in considering the damages caused by the admission of these independent telephones the destruction of the monopoly must be considered. I wish to say a few words upon one or two of the clauses of Bill No. 132, and to repept what I said on a former occasion with regard to the first section. The Minister of Justice will recollect that on a previous occasion I objected to the words in the fifth line giving the Privy Council power to rescind old orders made by the Railway Committee, and stating that in my opinion it would be proper, under the circumstances, to give the Privy Council power to validate orders that had been left in suspense, hung up between the two general railway Acts, but that I thought there was an objection to continuing in the Privy Council the power of varying and rescinding those old orders. The hon. gentleman said that the government had considered that question, and for some special reason they desired to continue in the Privy Council the power to deal with the old orders.
Well, I could understand that there might be some reason perhaps why, under a particular order such as he referred to-I think that one relating to Yonge street in Toronto-they might want to deal with it. But it does seem to me that they are likely to create a dual jurisdiction which might cause confusion by taking power to vary or rescind old orders, in the Privy Council, because section 33 of the Bill of last year gives to the Railway Commissioners power to deal with such matters. I think this should be reconsidered by the government before the Bill passes the Senate.
Now with regard to what may be called the Sunday observance clauses, I do not want to discuss here the merits of Sunday observance, or whether it is right to prohibit the use of street cars or electric railways in the cities of Canada on the Lord's day. But I think I am justified in calling the attention of the Minister of Justice to the very peculiar methods that have been adopted here in dealing with the question. This section 6a professes to validate laws existing in the various provinces, and parliament is asked to endorse those laws. Well, I think the Minister of Justice will have great difficulty indeed in telling the House precisely what those laws are that he has asked us to validate. I think there have been many attempts made to find out what they are, and I am not sure but that the question is now before the Supreme Court. It does seem to me rather peculiar that parliament should be asked to validate laws the provisions of which it is impossible at present for us to know. Now I would like the hon. the minister to consider that question. The whole subject is one of very great difficulty, and I would point out to him the peculiar position this parliament will be placed in after it validates the laws of the provinces. Parliament might hereafter change its mind and wish to alter, or extend, or in some way change those laws after having confirmed them, and I presume we will have no power here even to repeal what we have done, we will have settled the question once for all. As I said before, I do not want to deal with the question of Sunday observance, because I do not think this Bill brings up sufficiently the merits of that question. But it seems to' me that we are merely shuffling with the question, and we are putting both parties to the controversy, on the one hand those who are advoctes of the strictest observance of the Lord's Day, and on the other hand those who think there ought to be a little laxity for the convenience and accommodation of the people-we are putting them both, it appears to me, into a sea of litigation. After this Act is passed I doubt whether anybody will be one whit further advanced in his knowledge of what the law really is. I am told, I do not know whether it is true or not, that the question is now before the Supreme

Court, or is about to be submitted there. It occurs to me that it is in the interest of both parties that the law should first be settled, and that legislation should then pass in this parliament, if need be, to supplement or improve the legislation of the provinces. In any case the course proposed to be pursued here is a most extraordinary one, especially as regards subclause 2, whereby apparently we give to the government of the day power by Order in Council to validate laws that may hereafter be passed. I think it is a very grave question whether that is a proper form of legislation. We have a duty to perform as representatives of the people. To say that we now shall give what I called on a previous occasion a power of attorney to the gentlemen who happen to be ministers at a given moment, to approve laws that may hereafter be passed by another legislative body, does seem to me a very extraordinary course. I call attention to this, as I said before, without entering into the merits of the question, but merely to ask whether it is a proper thing for this parliament to do, or whether it can do it with any regard at all to its own obligations and its duties. With regard to the other two clauses concerning the Grand Trunk Pacific matter, the hon. gentleman accepted two amendments I offered the other day ; the third amendment that I proposed, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company having control of the Grand Trunk Pacific ought to be made to make good whatever loss the Grand Trunk Pacific might sustain by an improper apportionment of the rates, I think was a proper clause under the circumstances ; but I do not think there is any use occupying the time of the House in discussing a section that has already been voted down by the hon. gentlemen opposite.

I think that before legislation such as this contemplated in section 2 is placed before the House, the provincial enactments which are referred to should be scheduled as part of the Act. I am not dealing with the question of Sunday observance. I do not know what the Acts are which we are validating. They may be very wise Acts, They may be Acts to which I would not object if they were presented to the House. They may be Acts that I would thoroughly approve of, but it does seem to me that they should be scheduled and that we ought to know what we are dealing with. The subject that it dealt with is a very important subject. It is one, no doubt, upon which this parliament may be called upon to act, but it seems to me that the proper way to act is by legislation of our own. If we do not see fit to adopt that course, but rather to act in relation to the legislation of the provinces I am unhesitatingly of opinion that that legislation should be scheduled as part of the Act.
Subsection 2 of section 2 raises a ques-Mr. BARKER.
tion from the constitutional standpoint. It is a question which is not free from difficulty. It seems to be conclusively established by the judgments of the Supreme Court of Canada and of the Privy Council that a legislature, or parliament, can delegate only a matter over which it has jurisdiction, but I would think that under the constitution there must be some limit to that. For example, I do not think that the parliament of Canada can alter the constitution which has been conferred upon us by saying that in respect to nineteen or twenty subjects which are within the exclusive jurisdiction of parliament they shall be dealt with by the provincial legislatures in the respective provinces and that any legislation in respect to these subjects enacted by the provincial legislatures shall have the same force and effect as if enacted by this parliament. We cannot go that far ; we cannot destroy the constitution. Short of going that far it is a very serious question as to how far we can go. Under this legislation we seem to be going very far because we are authorizing the Governor in Council to ratify, as if passed by this parliament, legislation to be passed in the future by the different provinces of Canada. We are doing that in respect to a matter which has been held*to be one of criminal jurisdiction. If we can do this why can we not say that the whole criminal law of Canada shall in future be delegated to the different provinces, shall be administered under laws to be passed by each of the legislatures within the respective provinces over which the legislatures have control ? I do not see at present that the principle of the legislation which we have before us would be extended under an Act of that kind. We are taking one branch of what is held to be criminal law and we are saying that any law which is in the future passed by any of the provincial legislatures in regard to this subject shall be a good law upon one condition, namely, that it is ratified by the Governor in Council. It is a matter of some interest as to how far we can go and also a matter of considerable interest as to how far we should go in respect to a matter of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The point which was made by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) when he addressed the House before, did not strike me as clearly as it does now ; that is as to the right to rescind old orders. I did not catch this point at the time he put it before the House as clearly as I do now, but it is a question that deserves immediate attention on the part of the government in order to meet the difficulty which he has stated and which is a real difficulty I admit. The question in respect to Sunday legislation is not free from difficulty. I do not pretend for a moment that it is but I would like to put the question as it ap-

pears to me, as I think it may be fairly put before the House, and in a light in which I think it will meet with the approval of the House. We have taken out of the control of the provinces railways and works of that description which of their nature are merely local works and which, if they had remained, as they were intended to be, local in their character, would have been subject to provincial legislation in respect to the observance of Sunday. By virtue of the power which is conferred upon us by the Bi'itish North America Act we have declared these works, which are of their essence local works, to be works for the general advantage of Canada and as a result of that declaration they have passed from out the jurisdiction of the provinces to the jurisdiction of the federal authorities, so that while two railways may be in existence in a province operating side by side, both originally authorized under provincial charters, because one of them happens to have been declared a work for the general advantage of Canada it passes from out the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature, and the other one that has been created by the same authority continues on under the jurisdiction of the province. It seems to me that there is nothing illegal or unconstitutional in our declaring that while we are taking a work over for the general purposes of its administration and making it subject to our laws we desire that that work, in so far as its local operations are concerned and in so far as Sunday observance is concerned, shall remain under the jurisdiction of the legislature which created it. I do not think that there is anything in that which is improper. I would like to say that this legislation is not at all novel in its character. It is the same legislation that we have adopted in respect to our Franchise Act. We take the Act of the local legislature in respect to the franchise. We allow the legislature to determine the conditions under which the lists shall be made and we declare that those lists shall avail in so far as we are concerned, to that extent adopting the legislation of the provinces. It may be said very properly that this is legislation for which this government are responsible and that therefore we cannot appeal to a precedent created by ourselves. But, that was a precedent created immediately after confederation, because, up to 1885 when the Franchise Bill was passed, we adopted the provincial laws in respect to the making of the provincial lists and which provincial lists we made federal lists for the purposes of our federal parliament ; not only the lists as they stood at the time but we practically gave what my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) described as a blanket power of attorney to alter, change, and make the provincial lists and we contented *ourselves with adopting anything that the legislatures of the provinces did in that respect. So this legislation proceeds upon
the principle that was laid down at the time the Franchise Act was adopted.

Were the conditions not different in the case to which the hon. gentleman refers ? There we found ourselves in regard to our own franchises while here the hon. gentleman is binding the citizens of the provinces.

speechtext: The members of a corporation.
The members of the corporation as citizens.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As citizens of the provinces, but it seems to me that in respect of the Franchise Act by allowing each province to prepare the lists in the manner described we bound all those who were to avail themselves of those lists. We bound *the voters of this Dominion.
That was only a tentative matter to provide for an emergency until we adopted some other principle, or ' until such time as the parliament of Canada otherwise decides.'

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, parliament held to that principle a long time or until the change was made in 1885. In respect to subsection 2 of section 2 to which my hon. friend the leader of the opposition refers it is constantly the case that this parliament delegates to the Governor in Council power to make regulations and in connection with these regulations to enact penal legislation for the violation of these regulations. There has not been a session probably since confederation during which it has not been left open to the Governor in Council to make regulations which were more far reaching in their results than the action which would be taken by the Governor in Council on provincial laws with respect to Sunday observance. My hon. friends seem to be somewhat in error when they speak of Sunday observance as being a matter of criminal legislation. It is not a matter of criminal legislation. It is quite true that the Privy Council held that the Ontario Act was invalid because it affected to create a criminal offence, but the Privy Council did not decide that that Act was bad in toto. The Privy Council did not decide that the Act is bad in toto ; what they held was that the Act was bad in so far as it pretended to deal with criminal legislation. The questions to be referred to the Supreme Court are settled on, and I think it Will be found that the judgment of the Privy Council is susceptible of an entirely different construction from that which has been put upon it up to the present time. That judgment has been construed as taking from the provinces, powers which they are undoubtedly endowed with. I do not think the judgment ever was intended to take these powers from

tlie provinces and confer them on the Dominion parliament. When the judgment is carefully examined, it will be fount! I think, that all the Privy Council decided was, that with respect to these offences which are criminal in their nature, the provinces have no power to alter or amend the law with regard to them, nor have the provinces power to create an offence criminal in its nature. The Privy Council has not said that the provinces have not the right to determine the character of Sunday observance ; they have not determined that the provinces have not the right to say that a man shall work or shall not work on Sunday.
If the provinces have that right ; how is their right affected by the fact that certain property within the province is subject to the jurisdiction of this parliament ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The impression exists that in so far as works of a federal character are concerned, these works fall under the operation of Dominion legislation, and that the province has not the power to deal with them except in relation to contracts made within the province. But with respect to the control of these works which are of their nature provincial, it seems to me it is quite proper that while we take them over for federal purposes and declare them to be works for the general advantage of Canada, yet in so far as Sunday observance is concerned, they remain within the control of the provinces. 1 see no reason why they should not.

Suppose this parliament should incorporate a company to carry on a great industry in all the provinces, would the mere fact that we incorporated that company prevent the provincial laws from affecting persons employed by that company ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It has been well settled that the imoviuces have practically no control over the operation of railways, and the Sunday observance law is almost exclusively applicable to the operation of railways. If a railway becomes a federal railway under the operation of the federal law, it takes it from the control of the provinces. It is in that view' that this legislation is introduced.
If you incorporate a great smelting company or something of that kind, the fact that we incorporated it would not prevent the provincial law's affecting it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Quite so.
And it is on the ground that the operation of a railw'ay is under the jurisdiction of this parliament ?
