This is an opportune time for the minister to explain in what condition the question is with regard to the division of authority between the Dominion and the provinces with respect to the fisheries.

speakeroldname: Hon. RAYMOND PREFONTAINE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speechtext: No progress has yet been made except with regard to negotiations as to the basis of the submission of a case to the Supreme Court. I have already explained the matter this session. We have discussed the question w'ith the representatives of British Columbia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. The offer was that the federal government would take possession of the fisheries of the different provinces, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and British Columbia, under certain conditions. These conditions were discussed informally and the result as I stated at the time was that we agreed that if wre did not come to any agreement a ease w'ould be submitted to the Supreme Court. Mr. Pugsley and the premier of Prince Edward Island had to leave for England to be present at the argument of a case before the Privy Council a few days ago as regards the representation of these two provinces.
Would the minister give us some information about the contemplated establishment of a naval militia ?
In the supplementary estimates for 1901-5 there is a special, item for that and in addition it will be considered when the Bill now on the order paper is submitted for second reading.
The minister will make a statement then in respect to the establishment.
Within a few days I presume.

In connection with the large amount of money which is being appropriated for the protection of the fisheries and for fish hatcheries, I think that any one who goes to the rivers in Quebec and New Brunswick will find a general complaint that the regulations as to the taking up of nets for certain periods are not carried out and that the fishing in these rivers is decreasing in volume and extent each year. The money that is expended on fish hatcheries is a mere bagatelle compared to the damage done because the regulations are not properly carried out. I speak as an inland man, but as one having gone for many years down to the fishing sections and I believe that there are

very few people who have any idea of the value of these fisheries and of the importance of preserving the streams. In years to come this is going to be one of the most valuable assets of the province, and I can show the minister from my own experience and the experience of all those who fish on the rivers, both the Restigouche and other rivers, that three out of four of the fish caught in these rivers in many years are net marked, showing that they had had to struggle through the nets. Because the regulations as to taking up the nets are not enforced, the fishing on these streams as I have said, is decreasing in value year by year. I am not saying that the government are not doing as well as has been done in the past, but I think there should be some new regulation and some more stringent enforcement of the present laws or in a few years the salmon fishing will be destroyed. Americans go there and spend a large amount of money and the different districts of these rivers are enormously enriched.

I can tell my hon. friend that this question is not at all new to the department and is not new to me, as Minister of Fisheries. Last year I was somewhat of a novice in the question and had to get the necessary information, and I discovered that there was a good deal of friction between those who hold leases in these rivers and those who engage in the pursuit of fishing for a living. I tried to apply the rules and regulations. I knew that there was some complaint by some clubs that we were not severe and strict enough towards the fishermen and license holders. This year we took all the necessary precaution's in advance and I think there is no ground whatever for complaint. We have done all that was necessary to be done without going too far in order to protect these provincial rights, because, after all, they are provincial rights and do not interest us in such a degree as the rights of fishermen themselves, or those who have engaged in the industry. Of course we know perfectly well our obligations and know that we are obliged to have rules to protect these people who have leased these privileges from the different provinces for which some of them have paid very heavily, having considered that they were of great value. I know ror instance of a special case, the case of Mu Hill, who has rented a river and who had reasons to believe that at the estuary of the river there was more fishing than was necessary. In order to protect his rights-for he had paid for the property .$50,000 and I think is paying about $10,000 a year rental to the provincial government-and in order to give him all the advantages to which he was entitled instead of renewing the licenses at the estuary of the River St. John to the people who had enjoyed them for 50 years we put them up by tender, and I may say
to the committee that we had a good deal of difficulty in renewing the licenses at a satisfactory rental. I had a great deal of complaint from those especially interested in the fishing for the last fifty years but we succeeded in selling that license at such a price as was advantageous to the department and would satisfy those interested in the fishing of the St. John river so that there can be no complaint this year. As regards the Restigouche, we have a special launch patrolling the estuary to protect the rights of those wiho have rented that river. Of course 1 realize that at the beginning of the1 season the people interested in the lease were rather nervous and I received complaints that the launch had not arrived. As every one is aware the season was late this year, and the launch had not only to look after the fishermen and those with licenses along the estuary, but also those with licenses in the neighbouring waters. The launch took a few days more than usual to reach the river Restigouche, but as soon as she did reach the Restigouche all doubt, I think, disappeared and there has been no neglect whatever. As soon as she did reach it, all grounds of complaint disappeared. It was not due at all to the neglect of the department.
Did that refer to Mr. Hill's privilege ?

He is paying $10, * 000 a year.
Mr. OSLEiR. I am not speaking in the interests of Mr. Hill, but in the general interest of preserving the fishery. It is being destroyed every year steadily I speak from my own experience, when I say that five out of six of the fish caught in certain seasons show that they have come through the net and were scarred by it. I was at Matane a day or two this year. The men I employed told me without hesitation that the nets are not taken up according to regulations on Saturday night at six o'clock and kept up until Monday morning, but are left a long time in the water beyond the regulations. That is stated by the river men, and evidently there is too much netting, or there would be more free fish coming to the river than there have been the last two years. There is hardly a fish sometimes in the season not marked, which shows that the nets are not taken up.

I would like to draw attention to a question which I had on the paper three or four days regarding fishing licenses given to fish in the Lake Winnipeg and tributaries of the Nelson river. My information is that the exclusive rights to fish in the water of all the lakes north of Lake Winnipeg and tributary to the Nelson river have been given for a very small sum.

This question was answered the other day when first called,

but by error the answer was not entered in the proceedings. The answer is that no exclusive privilege was given. I can bring down the lease. It is an ordinary lease.
What is the lease ?

I would rather bring it down, because that would be more satisfactory than speaking from recollection, and I will bring it down to-morrow. Some privilege for fishing In a special way has been granted, but no exclusive privilege.
What about the lease for the fishing on James' bay ?
It is there yet.
Does not that lease give the company exclusive rights ?
Nothing has been done whatever under the lease given Mr. McNee.
Has the lease been cancelled, or is it the intention of the government to cancel it ?
It has not been cancelled, and no demand has been made to cancel it. The lease is yet in existence, but no fishing is going on.

Does the hon. minister think that giving fishing leases in that way is the proper thing ? In my opinion, it is very improper and unwise. We are giving a lease for many years of what belongs to the public, and are giving it, through political influence, for practically no consideration whatever. Surely the government must have by this time made up their mind whether they intend to cancel the lease or allow it to remain, and let the company take advantage of the privileges.

I will look into the lease and see whether it is possible to cancel it. I must state that all leases passed since I have been Minister of Marine and Fisheries contain the provision that if the privileges are not taken advantage of within a certain delay the lease becomes null and void.
I am informed that certain friends of the government have received the rights of exclusive fishing in the rivers I have mentioned for the sum of $10 per year.

I do not remember the figure, but if it be $10, they must have obliged themselves to spend a certain amount of money within a certain delay. Sometimes the lease is given at $400 or $1,000 per year without any special condition attached as to the amount of money to be spent, but in other cases leases are granted on condition that a certain amount shall be spent within a certain delay. A sum as high as $50,000 has been stipulated in some cases as the amount to be spent by the company which undertakes to exploit the fishing. In this case I do not know exactly the amount.

Would it not be better to let the item stand until the lease is brought down ? I understand that the right to fish has been also leased to another friend of the government on Lake Winnipegosis. That lease should be brought down at the same time. The hon. gentleman should explain the policy of the department, so that the public may understand what it really is. The public should know if it is the policy of the government to favour its friends by giving leases of that kind for the paltry sum of $10 a year, and then allowing them to sell their privilege to a fishing company. If the hon. minister will look into the matter, he will find that what I am telling him comes pretty near the mark. In ail these leases the men who get them have no intention of doing any fishing, but intend disposing of their rights.
As regards the two leases which the hon. gentleman has mentioned, I shall have them put on the table as soon as possible.	.
What benefit are those leases to the fishing interests of the district ? Are they in the interests of the fisheries or of the department ?

Of course, the leases will explain themselves. For myself I must say that I have never considered any other interest than that of the department and the public interest in granting these licenses and leases. Of course, I have always considered the fostering and development of the industry as important. If parties come to the government and say : We are ready to develop the fishery industry in such and such a section, and will bind ourselves to such and such conditions, then we eon-sider whether the conditions are favourable in the public interest and on that basis the lease is granted or refused. There is a fixed regulation with regard to licenses issued every year, but when it comes to granting licenses for a longer period than one year, the conditions vary ; the questions are settled on their merits, we using our best judgment in the interests of the industry.

I have no desire to press this matter now, so long as it is understood that an opportunity will be afforded for its discussion at a later time. Meantime I would like the leases of Mr. Arch. McNee, of .James' Bay, Mr. Merritt, of Lake Winnipegosis, and the other lessee whose name I do not know to the north end of lake Winnipeg, to be brought down.
I promised the hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyd) that he will have an opportunity to discuss the matter with the papers on the table.
Before this subject is dropped, I wish to say one word on the principle. It seems to me it is a bad principle to give leases to foreigners to take all the fish they like.
We have not granted leases to foreigners.

Whatever the form may be, these are practically leases to foreigners. The law happens to be that an American who catches fish in Canada can take them in to his own country free of duty, a privilege that is denied to a Canadian. But, on the other hand the American cannot get the fish here unless he associates himself with Canadians. The result is that the Canadians catch the fish, but when the fish go across the line they belong to the Buffalo Fish Company or some other concern who say they have the right to take them across the line free of duty, because they were caught by themselves. And so they'can get a better market than Canadians can get. That should not be allowed. If they were giving a good consideration for it, it would not matter so much. The minister says : But we develop the industry. But, what use is the development of the industry if there is no royalty ? And the royalty now is a mere nothing. We keep up the Fishery Department and establish fish hatcheries, and these Americans use our fisheries for their own purpose, giving us very little for the privilege. In connection with this fishery question we ought to have a general statement as to the policy of the government, and a statement as to whether they intend to give exclusive rights in any part of Canada which are practically monopolized by foreigners.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) must be under a false impression. There is only one company at all in the position he refers to. The fact is. this privilege granted to some Americans on the Pacific Coast was granted under very peculiar circumstances. It is not a license from the department, but simply an Order in Council authorizing an American Company-I think it is the New England Fish Company-to buy supplies and land their fish on the coast of British Columbia, and to ship fish in bond to their destination. The fish are caught in American waters.
I think the minister is not directing attention to the lease I refer to-the lease on James' Bay.
That has not been exploited.
But what I contend is that the principle of granting such leases is an unsound one. And we want him to bring down the lease so that we may see the provisions of it.

I promise to do that. I was going to explain the privileges given to the New England Fish Company on the Pacific Coast. I believe that the granting of these privileges of buying provisions and landing and shipping fish is a good move. The halibut fishery had not
been developed at all. There were large quantities of these fish in international waters, but they were not used because they were too far from American waters. Under the present arrangement this fishery can be developed. The advantage to Canadians is obvious. The company employ Canadian labour, buy their provisions from Canadian merchants, and pay large amounts in freight.
I understand that the first year the company paid over $100,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway for freights. The second year, they paid $200,000, and last year no less than $300,000. All this trade would have been lost to Canada if we had not consented to the arrangement. If Canadians would be as enterprising as to do the same thing, though they could not have the privilege of the American jnarkicjt as the citizens of that country have, they might be able to develop a market on our own side.
Would the minister say whether there is any fishery or other patrol belonging to the government now in the waters of Hudson Bay ?

None, except the ' Neptune,' which has been cruising there for the last year looking after Canadian interests and visiting the different posts so as to report to the Department of the Interior what means should be adopted to protect Canadian rights.
Has this government control over the fishery in Lake Winnipeg and Lake Winnipegosis ?
Yes.

These are entirely controlled by American companies. When you go to Winnipeg, you find considerable apprehension expressed among the public that these lakes will be overfished-in fact that ah the fish are being taken away.
That is not the information we have in the department. I think the business is not decreasing at all, but is maintaining itself.
The leases are entirely controlled by American companies.

Some of these companies, both Canadian and American are not fishing at all, but are buying from Canadian fishermen in the locality who hold licenses. This fact was brought to my attention by some members from the Northwest Territories.
I think the minister is mistaken. To my own knowledge American companies fish there largely, they have a supply of boats and a supply of men to an enormous extent, and have a large capital engaged.

The licenses are given to British subjects or Canadians,

57S0
sometimes organized into joint stock companies. It sometimes happens that American capitalists put their money into these companies and, obtaining control of the stock, they become American companies. But I do not see how we can help that by legislation or by regulations.

It is not so much that 1 complain of, but in some places the fishing has practically ceased now, the whole industry has gone. When I was in Winnipeg I heard the subject discussed and heard it stated several times that the wholesale catch of fish was practically destroying the fishing in those lakes, just as the sturgeon fisheries have been destroyed.

Whether these fish are caught by Canadians or Americans does not make much difference. If they had been caught by Canadians the depletion of which the hon. gentleman complains would have resulted in the same way. But that is not ' the case. The information of the department is that these lakes are not being depleted. Of course we can understand that in lakes with shallow water where a good deal of fishing is going on, the fish are driven away into more remote places. The same thing has happened in the St. Lawrence. I remember when, twenty or twenty-five years ago, a good deal of fish of all sorts was caught around the island of Montreal, but now you can scarcely catch fish there of any consequence. It is the same everywhere. As settlements are established about the lakes, especially those with shallow water, the fish seek new haunts where they are less disturbed. But the regulations are duly followed, and all precautions are taken in order to preserve the fisheries.
How many inspectors are there on these two lakes to protect the fisheries V
I think there are four in the west. They are Henry McKay, Cedar Lake ; A. J. McPherson, Dauphin, Man.; James Silverthorne, Lumsden, Assa., and J. F. Healson, Prince Albert.
One at Dawson and one at Cedar Lake have all this enormous stretch of waters to look after north of Lake Win-nipegosis.
I am asking this year for more money to have a better inspection made. Early this spring I sent one of my officers to report hoW| many are required and what methods are adopted.
What is the object of having a fishery officer at Cedar Lake or within two hundred miles of it ?
They were put there before I came into the department
because, I suppose, that was the proper place to put them.
The minister says it is immaterial whether .these fish are caught by Americans or by Canadians. Is that a fact ?
So far as the depletion goes.
But does it not make some difference with regard to getting the fish into the American market ? If Americans catch the fish they take them into the American market free of duty.

I do not s^e why they should go Into the American market free of duty.
Mr1. GANONG. Americans of easy conscience are fishing along the eastern seaboard who carry their fish into the United States market free of duty, and I thought perhaps there were some up west afflicted in the same way. I can correct the minister in regard to one thing ; I think Mr. Hill's fishing territory is not on the river St. John, it is oh some of the northern waters.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is in the seigniory of Mingan. _
What are the duties of the fishery overseer at Lumsden, and what fish does he look after there 7 There is but very little fish there.

It is a fact, whether the minister knows it or not, that fish caught by Americans are going into the United States market free. I know that the Buffalo Fish Company was organized for the purpose of fishing in Georgian bay, and they have been getting their fish into the American market free of duty. If Americans fish in Candian waters the catch can be taken into the American market free of duty, but if Canadians catch the fish and endeavour to get them in United States they have to pay duty on them. Therefore, though Canadians may supply the boats, if the fish are caught under the name of an American firm, they go into the American market free of duty. I think that is a wrong to Canadians because there are many Canadians fishing in the Georgian bay who have to compete with Americans, and they cannot send their product over the line without paying duty. They are denied that right, while Americans fishing alongside of them get the benefit of the United States market. The same principle I am told is being exercised by this American company that is fishing in Hudsons bay and several other places. The same question arose in Newfoundland a short time ago where a firm of Americans are storing ice, or are about to establish ,an industry there, and it appears that there is a provision in the American customs law which allows them

access to the United States market free of duty. I have no doubt that the Americans who are fishing in Lake Winnipegosis are doing the same thing, and their fish are going free to Minneapolis and St. Paul, while Canadians fishing in the same waters are denied that right.
I know that American fishing companies operating on the north shore of Lake Superior get their fish free into the American Sault.
On page 197 of the fisheries report of 1903, you will find the report of Mr. Young, inspector of fisheries for that district.
Have you reports from your officers in different districts ?
Yes, from different places where there is fishing going on.
In the Northwest Territories ?
In the Northwest Territories. The fisheries in the Northwest are covered by the report of Mr. Miller.
These are officers for the whole country ?

We have the reports of these officers and we have reports from their sub-officers. The reports from the Northwest Territories commence at page 202 of the Annual Report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Beginning at that page will be found a synopsis of reports received from the different districts.
What is the report from the Lumsden man ?

Mr. Miller the inspector reports as follows :
In Long lake the fishing was about the same as in former years. Overseer Silverthorne reports that large catches of whitefish were made just before the commencement of the close season, the fish seeming to come into the shallow waters rather early. It may become necessary to close this portion of the lake to prevent the destruction of spawning fish. This lake too has gained during the year though still much below its one time level.
In the Qu'Appelle river and the smaller streams the long continued high water afforded small opportunity for the illegal trapping of fish during the spring close season and though some fish weirs were discovered and destroyed by guardians, as a rule they are now only met with in the vicinity of new foreign settlers unacquainted with the law.
If I understood the hon. minister correctly he stated that fish caught on the Pacific coast could be entered in Victoria and shipped in bond to the United States. Am I correct ?

I am afriad I have not made myself understood. I did not state anything of the sort. I stated that fish caught in international waters, on the high sea, by this New England Fish Company, to whom the privilege was granted of buying their provisions and landing on Canadian soil could, according to certain arrangements made with the American government, be shipped in bond and delivered in Boston. The fish are not Canadian fish. They are caught in international waters.

That is still more extraordinary. This American company can come into British waters on the Pacific coast, catch all the fish they like, ship them over a British railway to the United States and sell them there. I knew the law was against them if the fish were caught in American waters or in waters other than British waters, because then they would have no right to come into the port of Victoria or ship the fish over a British railway to the United States. If they had that right what would be the use of our fisheries on the Atlantic coast ? American fishermen could go on the banks off the coast of Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island, catch fish, ship them by the same means as those employed by our own fishermen and send them free of duty to the United States when our own fishermen would have to pay duty going into the United States ? It would transfer our whole fishing trade from Canadian fishermen to United States fishermen. But, they get around it on the Pacific coast. You can form a company of Americans and they can come and fish in our own waters.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon.
Well, I did not clearly understand the minister.

I do not know how it is that I have not made myself understood because I have repeated it twice. I said that the fish are not caught in Canadian waters at all. They are caught outside of the three-mile limit in international waters.

I understand perfectly now. They are caught in waters which are not Canadian waters. Then, the fisherman of Nova Scotia, when he catches fish outside of the three-mile limit, can come into Halifax and ship them into the United States ?
He has not applied for that privilege yet.	.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon ?
No fisherman in Nova Scotia has applied for that privilege yet probably because the fishermen in Nova Scotia have not to back them such a large company as the Canadian Pacific Railway.
I have listened to the debates in this House long enough to know that the Nova Scotia fisherman has no right to do it.
Everybody knows that.

Perhaps it is because of some denseness on my part that I do not understand the hon. minister. He says that these iish are caught outside of Canadian waters, that they are caught in waters in which the fishermen of the whole world can fish and that these fish are then brought into Victoria. Why does not the same principle apply to Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island ? We have only controlover three miles from the coast line. If flsb are caught outside of the coast line why cannot they be brought into Halifax or Sydney, shipped over the railway and entered at a United States port free of duty ?

I do not wish to keep the committee back but I would like to say a word or two in connection with the New England Fish Company operating on the Pacific coast. Prior to their coming into our waters there was no halibut caught and there was no halibut industry. I he New England Fish Company which control about 300 retail stores throughout the New England states came into the Pacific waters and asked to have the privilege of shipping through a Canadian port, the port of Vancouver, to their market in Boston and the New England states. They received that privilege upon one consideration and that consideration was that they were to employ entirely Canadian workmen, they were to buv entirely Canadian goods, and to operate the industry as far as the catching of the fish was concerned entirely in our interest.
Who had the authority to make any such arrangement with them ?
Why, our government'.
They have no power to do that.
Well, they are doing it.
That is what we want to find out.
They are doing it and it is a proper thing to do.
That is another question.
I am not speaking of the authority, under the law'. It is the fact that I am speaking of.
I have heard of this arrangement for the first time this evening.

If these Americans had not come in we would not have had the halibut fishery developed as we have. I want to give an illustration to show how government interference can do a great deal of harm. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) spoke of the sturgeon fisheries of the northern lakes. In 1892 an American company came over to the Fraser river and prepared to develop the sturgeon fisheries. They had a large market for these fish in the city of Chicago, they employed two steamers, they had forty or fifty men working for them, and they employed entirely white labour. They were catching sturgeon and shipping them out. The industry had never been started before in our waters. They were taking the sturgeon from the mud banks of the Fraser. In one night a breath came from Ottawa that they must stop fishing sturgeon because they would deplete the fish. The result is that there has been no sturgeon industry in those waters from that time to this so that this important industry was knocked on the head. It does not matter whether it is an American company or Canadian firms who are doing the fishing. We want the fishing industry developed and if Americans choose to take advantage of the opportunities by engaging in the industry and if they take the fish that are caught by our fishermen and which are hauled over our railway, I do not see why we should object. There must be two sides to every question and the Americans must have some advantage. I would like to see our own money invested in this industry but our people do not seem to be alive to the fact that we have such an immense industry in Canada and that there is a possibility of making a lot of money out of the fisheries. Our people do not seem to be so thoroughly alive to the fact as the Americans are. I am strongly of the impression that the government acted wisely and well when they gave to the New England Fish Company these advantages.
It follows that the whole Canadian fishing industry could pass from Canadian into American hands.
Not at all.

Does the hon. gentleman object to the industry which is being conducted upon our coast ? I do not think he does.
* Mr. HAGGART. I do not know anything about it but I do not know where the government get the authority under the law to do it.
Yes, because if you can do it on the Pacific coast you can do the same thing on the Atlantic coast.
Canadians are getting the benefit.

The net result is that the whole of our fishing industry will pass

into American liands, and their fish can go into the United States free of duty while ours will have to pay duty.
Has the fish commissioner made any report in regard to licenses along the eastern sea-board ?
Their work is not yet finished and they have not made a final report.

It is remarkable that one lawyer, one colonel of militia, one editor, and, I think one fisherman, should be appointed by this government to inquire into the fishing industry worth $15,000,000 a year. It is also remarkable that when an election was expected the commission should be sent out hurriedly, and that when the Grand Trunk Pacific failed to put up the money they were called off again. In the east this fishery commission is looked upon as nothing but a farce.
Will the minister bring us down the Order in Council permitting this American company to land and cure their fish in Canada ?

This is a special arrangement with the New England Fish Company renewable yearly by an Order in Council on the report of the Minister of Customs allowing the fish to pass through Canada in bond. The order has always been issued with the approval of the Department of Fisheries. I never saw the American company or their representative in connection with the matter, but those who asked for a renewal were Canadians, and the authorities of the Canadian Pacific Railway who were specially interested. I believed it was in the public interest to continue this privilege as long as they were the only ones in the field.
Did you consult the Minister of Justice as to your power to pass this Order in Council ; when was it first passed ? 1
In 1890 when Sir Louis Davies was minister.
You are doing by Order in Council what you are only empowered to do by treaty.
I do not think the Minister of Customs will have any objection to bring down the Order in Council.
I ask the Minister of Justice whether this government has power to pass such an Order in Council ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not seen the Order in Council and I cannot answer as to its validity.
This thing is illegal, and I believe it is contrary to the national interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is nothing contrary to the national interest in allowing fish to be landed on our shore, and carried through to the United States in bond.

This is not a Canadian industry in the first .place. If Canadians went outside the three-mile limit and caught halibut they would do so in Canadian bottoms ; _and the Americans would take good care that fish so caught would have to pay duty. The Americans catch these fish on the high seas in American bottoms, and so they escape the American duty, but they employ Canadian labour and buy their supplies in Canada.
That could be done on the Atlantic coast.
It could, but only under modus vivendi licenses.

I will not set myself up as a constitutional authority, but I* do not think the order would have passed Council if it were illegal. Canadians could not engage in this business under equal conditions. By permitting this Order in Council to be renewed from year to year we give away none of our rights, and this fishing company trades with the merchants of Vancouver and ships their freight over the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Order in Council is passed in the interests of Canada and Canada alone. We could repeal the Order in Council any day, but we would lose a great deal of business in consequence.
We are giving these people a right which otherwise they would not enjoy, and by doing the same thing on the Atlantic coast you could give the Atlantic fisheries over to the Americans.
That is regulated by treaty.
We have never attempted to give away such rights unless by treaty, and I believe this Order in Council is passed without authority.

I have never heard any objection from a Canadian source. If this Order in Council were not renewed, Canadians would not be employed; the merchants of Vancouver would not be traded with, and the Canadian Pacific Railway would not receive the earnings it does. I am sure that there will be no objection to placing the Order in Council upon the table and 'that when the subject is fully considered, no hon. gentleman opposite would take the responsibility of saying that we should not do what we have done.
Building and maintenance of fish-breeding establishments and lobster hatcheries, including the salary of F. H. Cunningham, $2,000, superintendent of fish culture, whose transfer from inside division without prejudice to his status under the Civil Service Superannuation Act is hereby ratified, $110,000.

Hr. SPROULiE. I understood the minister to say last year that he had decided to establish a fish hatchery on the Beaver river, close to the Georgian Bay. That is in every way a suitable location, and I would ask the minister if anything has been done or will he done in this matter ?

The department intended to establish a hatchery somewhere around the Beaver river, but last year the session was so long and there were such diverse interests as regards the site of this hatchery that the matter was suspended for further consideration. I intended either going myself or having some of my officials go to visit these localities and decide what would be the best place for this and many other hatcheries.. I intend to adopt this course in regard to the maritime provinces, and I shall leave next week for British Columbia for a similar purpose. In this case, I think we will be in a position to decide within a few weeks.
Is it intended to establish a lobster hatchery on the Bay of Fundy coast of New Brunswick '!

The fishing industry in the county which I have the honour to represent is very large and important. A great number of persons are employed in it, and I would ask how it is that the Minister of Marine has overlooked that important county and given us no fish hatcheries at all ? I think we are entitled to one at least. We represent the largest amount of capital of any county in the way of exports, and I think we are entitled certainly to some recognition. I would ask the minister to carefully consider that. I am not asking for favours ; I am asking for rights.

As I have explained in relation to the establishment of hatcheries in western Ontario, as well as in other parts of the Dominion, the reason for the delay is the fact that the session last year was so late that the only little trip I could take to the maritime provinces was one to Prince Edward Island in older to settle if possible the difficult question of the ferry to the mainland. I intend to do so as soon as the time is available for me, and I promise the hon. gentleman that I shall not fail to visit his locality.
Mi'. KAULBACH. I think if the minister will carry out his promise and visit my county, my statement will be fully verified, and he will have a very favourable impression of the county. I hope that in the future it will receive the benefits it so richly deserves.
Is this extra $30,000 in the supplementary estimates to be expended on the hatcheries already established, or is it proposed to open new fish hatcheries during the year ?
It is to provide for new ones.
Where ?
When the item of $30,000 is up I shall be in a position to give the information.

What proportion of this $110,000 goes to the new ones ?
Fisheries-oyster culture, $7,000.
Would the hon minister give us a little explanation ?
The annual report for 1903 gives much better explanation than I possibly could.
In what location is this money to be expended ?

In Caraquet Bay, N.B., at Malpeque, Prince Edward Island, at the Shediac oyster reserve.
Mi-. GANONG. Is any of this money to be devoted towards planting new beds in any other locality ?
We are waiting for a report from Mr. Kent, who is in charge of this culture, before deciding at what other places we will plant.
Is oyster culture encouraged'on the Bay of Fundy shore and the Atlantic shore ?

We have no oyster beds there. There are some in Annapolis, but they are small.
Fisheries-to assist in the establishment, maintenance and inspection of cold storage for bait for deep sea fishermen, under conditions to be fixed by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, $25,000.

I would move to have this item amended so that it may read as follows :
To assist in the establishment, maintenance and inspection of cold storage for deep sea fishermen, including assistance in the conservation and development of deep sea fisheries, under conditions to be fixed by the department.
The idea is not only to contribute a sum of money for the establishment of cold storage for bait for the deep-sea fishermen, but also to assist in preparing the fish by providing driers. The said amount of fj>25,000 has never been entirely spent in aiding cold storage for bait, and the department has ccme to the conclusion that by giving driers for fish at certain places, where there is a good market, that would help the deep-sea fishermen very materially. The driers would cost about $1,800. We are installing one at Souris in Prince Edward Island.
What class of drier is the bon. gentleman putting in ?
It is the drier manufactured by Collas, Whitman & Company. They hold the patent.
Is there any acetylene gas used in this cold storage ?
I do not think so.
Is there an item on which we could discuss that ?
Yes, the increased vote for lighthouses.
Is the system carried on and receiving aid from the government under a chemical process or the ordinary ice storage ?
Real ice is employed.

Has the minister recognized and thought favourably of the method of Eaton, which I detailed the other evening at some length ? The party is now in the city, and if the government would interview him, they would be able to receive
very much useful information which may lead up to an improvement in the present system.
I have no objection at all. If the hon. gentleman will present to me the person in question, he will be well received and I will .listen to any explanation he can give.
How much of the $25,000 voted for cold storage for bait for deep sea fishermen is to be diverted to the new service of building the drier ?
About $1,800 per drier.
How many driers ?
We will have them at places where we think they will be required. The first place where a drier will be installed is Souris, P.E.I.
Is that intended to take the place of the $25,000 the hon. minister has voted ?

No ; as I have explained this $25,000 though available on certain conditions has not been spent year after year. Only about half of it has been spent-$12,000 or $13,000. The boards of trade and the representatives of the fishermen have made representations that a certain amount of this vote could be diverted to the building of fish driers. It is somewhat in the same line and is intended to help the deep sea fishermen. After considering the matter we came to the conclusion that it would be a good idea, so we decided that at certain places where they bring their fish to be cured we would establish driers. These driers provide a mechanical means of effecting the curing of the fish which was formerly done by the sun and wind.
In fact, the hon. minister has been exercising his ingenuity to find means of spending this $25,000.
Exactly-in the interests of the fishermen.

The experience has been that fish driers, if used . to dry fish as they come out of the pickle or out of the pile ready to be put on the flake, have not been successful, but that driers used to dry fish that are already partially dried by the sun. are most successful. They have been tried in Halifax both ways by drying what we call green fish-which has not proven a success-and by drying fish already partially dried in the sun, which has been very successful.

Some hon. members present may not understand the conditions of the fish market. While I am not a fisherman, I know something about the matter.

It is solely in the interest of the export trade and these fish driers are built to prepare fish properly to go to the West India market, where the atmospheric conditions are very trying. From time to time, fish that are sun-dried and sent to that market turn out badly from sweating and mildewing. But, as I understand, the process suggested by the minister, by the use of what is known as the Whitman drier, has been an immense success, and a large business has been built up with the West Indies in fish cured by this process.

I am sure the minister will recognize the fact that my county, Lunenburg, has the largest fishing industry in the export trade, not excepting Halifax, Halifax exports fish, but the greater portion of it is fish from outside counties, particularly from Lunenburg. If there is any aid given to fish driers, evidently the county of Lunenburg is entitled to some of that aid. As the hon. member for Victoria (Hon. William Ross) has just explained, this is simply a process to carry the drying of fish further than it can be carried by means of the wind and sun. To take the fish green, as we call it, and put them through the drier would be rather to injure them for the market, because it would deprive them to a certain extent of their flavour. But when fish already partly dried in the sun are put through the mechanical drier, they can be sent in marketable shape to any part of the world. I think that, under the circumstances, the hon. minister will see that what I say is reasonable, and is in the interest of the fishermen as a whole, and that, as my county exports more largely than any other, he should recognize that fact and act accordingly.

In conversation with Mr. Whitman, who was here some few weeks ago, I got from him some information which does not accord with the statements made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kaulbach) who has just taken his seat. Mr. Whitman gave me to understand that it was possible to take the fish green, take them just as they come out of the water, and cure them completely by his method ; and that you could very successfully cure them by taking them out [DOT] of kench and putting them into the drier. Of course, the better way would be to partially cure them in the sun and wind and then complete the work in the drier. But, if the conditions would not allow that to be done, it was possible, as he had proven by practical experience. to cure them completely by putting them in the drier on taking'them out of kench-the conditions to which my hon. friend from Victoria refers-or even by taking them green altogether. All along the coast of the maritime provinces, particularly, I know so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned, we can get fish in the I Mr. GANONG.
fall of the year, even in October and November when it it not possible to dry them outside, the weather conditions not being suitable for curing them. It is then that the drier would be very useful. The fish caught at that season of the year can be cured by this means. But the drier would be useful also at other seasons when the fishermen are so busy, particularly if the catches were so good that they would not have time to complete the cure of thd fish on the flakes. They could then be placed in the drier and finished. And as the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Ganong) has said, this method has proven very successful for curing fish for the West Indian market where the climatic conditions are very trying. The curing of fish intended for that market has to be carried further than can be done under natural conditions of sun and wind. The fish have to be made harder, firmer, to stand the West Indiafi climate. In preparing fish for that market the driers have been very successful and as my hon. friend (Mr. Ganong) has stated a very successful trade has been built up by the Whitmans in curing their fish in this way. So far as I can obtain information on the subject, the driers, wherever they have been used, are very successful, and their operation will be a great assistance in the development of the fisheries.

I understand that the information given by the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. J. Hughes) was received from Mr. Whitman. While that statement might have be made to my hon. friend, at the same time Mr. Whitman is wrong. There have been cases in which the fish have been taken right from the catch after being salted and pressed, and put through this drying process and shipped. But it has been shown that they have to be put under such pressure-in order to get the moisture out of them and fit them for the drier-that a large portion of the nutritive properties of the fish is extracted, and it deteriorates the value of the fish, and lessens its price in the foreign market. I make this statement on the authority of shippers, and believe it to be true. Mr. Whitman, the originator and owner of the patent, would naturally be inclined to place all the advantages of his patent before the public. I am advised that the fish lose their virtue to a certain extent in the patent process of drying, if they are put under pressure sufficient to prevent the elimination of the moisture.

A large drying establishment based on the Whitman process was put up in Halifax, and they had to abandon the drying of green fish altogether. There is no green fish dried in that drier now. The drier is used to harden fish that have already been dried by the sun, in that case the system is successful. Thlis' process may be used in drying fish for the-

West Indies or for South American trade when they are received by the merchants partially dried. But there is no process in the world equal to the sun drying to make good fish, and my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach) will bear out that testimony.
Fisheries-to provide for the maintenance of the Georgian Bay laboratory, $1,500.
This is a station for a commission devoted to the study of the fishing industry. It is no invention of mine.
Has this commission a headquarters or station where they meet to discuss matters, or is it a kind of roving commission ?

They meet twice a year to study and discuss these matters in the interests of fishermen, and they publish every two years a report of their work. In the summer they are stationed on the Georgian Bay. This money is to pay their expenses, to provide a boat house in which they live on the Georgian Bay. Their station is on the Richmond Bay, above Midland. There is also a station in Prince Edward Island.

That is by statute.

I referred to that item the other day, and I would like to ask the minister now if he is prepared to give an increased amount of fishing bounties this vear I think it would be reasonable to do so in view of the fact that the number of fishermen is considerably larger than it was when this amount was first granted. I think they are entitled to a larger amount for general distribution.

This amount is fixed by statute, and when the government considered this matter they came to the conclusion that without more consideration it was not opportune to increase this year the amount for bounties by statute.

The hon. gentleman will see that the amount at first was $150,000, and it was increased to $160,000. The additional amount being also made a statutory allowance. I think in view of the increased number of men engaged in fisheries the minister might well provide an additional amount this year.

We have not seen our way clear to make an increase.

Could not the minister succeed in getting the steamer ' Alert ' on

The suggestion is worth consideration. Instead of leasing a boat as we have been in the habit of doing to supply the lighthousees in the upper St. Lawrence we might use that boat for the purpose.

The boat is a large one, and suitable for the purpose. Now that all the other works have been completed and the hon. minister has taken over some of the vessels that are used by the Department of Railways and Canals, there is no reason *why lie should not take over the ' Alert.

Yes, I know ; but it was connected with the same department, the Department of Railways and Canals.
Ocean and river service-to pay amount of damages awarded merchants and shippers for losses sustained on perishable goods, owing to the detention of the ' Minto ' and Stanley by ice, $9,562.18,
Where was that ?
That happened during the winter of 1902-3.
Between the mainland and Prince Edward Island ?

Between the mainland and Prince Edward Island. The two boats were caught in the ice. Although we did not consider the claimants entitled in law to the amounts which have been allotted to them, we thought that these were fair and reasonable claims for the actual losses suffered by reason of the fact that these boats were caught in the ice. We sent a special officer to examine into these claims and he has reported. We were disposed to pay the amount without coming before parliament, but after due consideration we thought it would be better to lay the whole matter before the House, so that any explanation that might be required could be given.
The hon. minister, of course, knows that when you ship goods the dangers of navigation are accepted, so that in that case the government are not liable.
In law we are not liable, but this is a moral claim.

In this case the government can see then- way clear to paying these claims, but the right hon. Prime Minister is not able to see his way clear to paying the claim of the clergyman which I brought to his attention the other evening.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I desire to draw the attention of the hon. minister to the fact that in the county I have the honour to represent there is a larger number of young men than in any other part of the province engaged in the merchant marine service, and whilst a number of these young men are employed in the summer time in the prosecution of the industry of fishing, they are employed in the later autumn and winter in foreign service. There is a large amount of material that can be utilized were there a school established in the county, and I would ask the hon. minister if he would kindly look into that matter seriously. I spoke of it before, and I think it is a reasonable request that a school bo opened in the town of Lunenburg, where there are experienced ship masters who would be a credit to the service, and who would give valuable aid in advancing these young men to the positions of masters and mates, but who are now kept in the background for the want of a local school. I would ask the hon. minister in all seriousness to give his careful attention to the subject and to have a school opened in the county. There is another matter to which I would like to call the attention of the hon. minister. For some years the coast service was extended down to the West Indies, while now it has its limit at Cape Hatteras. Although these young men have not the authority to sail foreign as well as coastwise, they go out boldly as well as those who are possessed of the natural qualities of seamen and who are authorized to cross the Atlantic. In a measure they have the experience, because thev have been sailing to the West Indies. Their calling is to the West Indies, because a large portion of the fish caught in the summer time are carried in the winter time to the West Indies for a market. I feel satisfied that if the hon. minister would extend the limit of the coast service to the West Indies, as it was in the past, it would be an advantage.

That question is receiving the special attention of the chairman of the Board of Masters and Mates, and we hope to be able to remedy the existing state of affairs. As regards an examiner at Lunenburg, I may state that there is one at Yarmouth and one at Halifax. The distance is not very great, but, all. the same,
I will have a report made upon the subject.
These men desirous of qualifying are of a class who are hardly able to bear the expense of going to Yarmouth, which is a long way off, or even going to Halifax in the adjoining county.
In certain cases, where there are three or four together, we send the examiner to the place so that they many be examined.

I am aware of the fact that they are examined at the present time, but still there is no school. Were

there a school they would be able to acquire knowledge of the details to an extent which would advance them much more rapidly than by adopting the rude process that they have at the present time ; that is, going up for examination before the parties who are appointed by the board.
Lighthouse and coast service - further amount required for the construction and completion of the Lurcher and East Point Anticosti lightships, $15,000.
Explain.

This will settle the account for the construction of these two light ships. They were contracted for by my predecessor, built by the Poison Iron works and are the most modern lightships in the world.
Lighthouse and coast service-maintenance and repairs to lighthouses, $35,000.

Last year's vote of $345,000 was exhausted on the first of June. A great number of these lighthouses were bdilt before confederation and needed extensive repairs. A large number received new apparatus ; the severe winter entailed extra expense at the request of the shipping interests of Montreal the buoys were left in the channel later than usual and some of them were lost, and had to be replaced ; this spring a number of the buoys were carried away.
Will acetylene be put in all the lighthouses between Montreal and Kingston and the lighthouse-keepers done away with.
This vote is to supplement the expenditure between Montreal and Quebec.
I will require the reports of your officers as to the use of acetylene gas in these lighthouses. I refer especially to the reports of Mr. Anderson.

I will bring all the documents down on the supplementary estimates.
Lighthouse and coast	service-further
amount required for construction of lighthouses and aids to navigation, $50,000.

There have been some statements made regarding the purchase of the property for the establishment of a lighthouse depot at Prescott, and I wish to say that I consider that property was bought very reasonably and cheaply, and the purchase of it was all right. There is another lot adjoining that property and if the government do not purchase it the whole look of the property they have will be spoiled. I hope the minister will see his way to purchase that lot and make the property square. I hope he will secure the adjoining lot.

This matter is under consideration. I have never been to
Prescott, but I hope to visit it soon, and 1 will look into this matter. I think $1,000 was asked for the adjoining lot, and I offered $500 and the owner is ready to sell for $750.

I think myself the lot is worth $1,000, and the government is not paying any too much for it even at that price. It is a corner lot and it will help to make the government lot more uniform, and the minister should not hesitate to buy it and make their lot complete.
Lighthouse and coast service-to provide for the purchase of a wharf for steamers and lighthouse service at Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, $13,000.
Explain.

When I visited Charlottetown last fall, I found that the ferry boats and government steamers had no proper wharf accommodation. The wharfs which our steamers used were really a disgrace. It was pointed out that we might buy the Poole property, and I was told that the price would be $16,000 or $18,000, I said we were not disposed to pay so high a price, and after a good deal of bargaining $13,000 was settled on, which is considered by everyone as reasonable and fair. It is without exception the best wharf in Charlottetown and besides we save $500 a year.
Did the government steamers land at that wharf before 1
No ; it was private property.
Has the government the exclusive right now ?

Yes.

The actual expenditure of the department is $105,000, and we have always overlapped to the extent of $20,000. To cover this deficiency we have to vote this $20,000.
I do not understand that system of bookkeeping. Here is $20,000 additional required for salaries and disbursements. How has the minister made the mistake ?

This year I am asking for the same amount of $20,000 to cover the amount which I am short for 1903-4.

Some one must have expended $20,000 more than he had a right to. Who was the minister who did that ?

tions with respect to any work or class of works conferred upon the Minister of Public Works by any of the Acts relating to harbour, commissioners, be transferred to and hereafter exercised by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.	-

That all moneys voted by parliament to either the Department of Public Works or that of Railways and Canals for the purpose of , carrying out any of -the works under the control of either department and now' transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, be placed to the credit of the last named department.
