When the committee rose at six o'clock the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prefontaine) had just read the Order in Council, which, under the statute passed last session, attributes certain of the duties of the Department of Railways and Canals and of the Department of Public Works to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. It reminds me of the campaign of the hon. minister in the division of Maisonneuve, when he presented himself for re-election after his acceptance of his present portfolio. I merely wish to call my hon. friend's attention to this and to ask for a word or two of explanation which, no doubt, he will give. At that time, my hon. friend will remember, it was charged by those opposed to his re-election that the important Department of Public Works had been taken away from the province of Quebec to which it had been allotted at the time of the distribution of portfolios in 1896, and that the department given to the province as represented by my hon. friend (Mr. Prefontaine) was a department of minor importance. I think that was a legitimate objection to raise in an election when all questions of public interest can he discussed, particularly an election which took place after a ministerial reconstruction. My hon. friend made a very good defence-so good that he was elected by a large majority. Amongst other things, he stated as he will remember, that the department which he was called upon to preside over, if he were elected, will undergo a very large development. That department, he said, would be entrusted with the superintendence of all navigation of every kind-[DOT] to use his own language-from the Yukon to the Atlantic ocean. What was understood by that was that there was going to be introduced a very important modifica-

tion of the system that had obtained since confederation in the organization of the administrative work of the Dominion. We understood that the Department of Marine and Fisheries was going to take from the Department of Public Works everything which concerned navigation, the construction of wharfs, the deepening of rivers, canal navigation-I believe that was specified at the time by my hon. friend and by his organs,-everything that concerned navigation, including the construction, repairs and labour of every kind. That was a new principle, that is, a new principle here, though not new as applied to other nations. The system which prevails here as hon. members of the committee know, is that the Department of Public Works is entrusted with all work of material construction throughout the Dominion, with whatever department it may be concerned. If the Department of Militia desires to have a drill hall erected, it is the work of the Public Works Department to construct it ; if a post office is to be erected, or a customs house built, or a building provided in connection with the Department of Justice or the Department of Trade and Commerce, -any building of whatever kind-it is supposed to be the work of the Public Works Department which is manned by a minister and a sufficient number of officials to carry out all the public works of the Dominion. And that it was which made that department in the eyes of the electors of Maison-neuve such an important department ; and that was why they, or at least a certain number of them, could not see why that department should be taken from the province of Quebec.
But the point to which I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is this : After my hon. friend had become a minister, he endeavoured to carry out the pledges he had made to his electors, I will give him credit for that. He made a noble effort to draw into his department everything that he said he would include in it. That he failed to realize his promises there is no doubt, and that is the point upon which I would like an explanation from him. There has evidently been a struggle, there has evidently been a conflict, and the Order in Council which my hon. friend read to us a short time ago is the outcome of that conflict. By the terms of the Order in Council the Department of Marine and Fisheries is charged with the St. Lawrence ship channel, it has charge of the localities that are under the control of harbour boards. Why is the attribution so restricted ? That is what I would like my hon. friend to explain. Take for instance, the navigation between Montreal and Quebec. My hon. friend, under the terms of this Order in Council, has charge of the ship channel from Montreal to Quebec where important works are going on ; he has charge of the construction of Mr. MONK.
piers and of public works to be executed within the harbour of Montreal, in that particularly restricted locality where the Harbour Commissioners have jurisdiction ; he has also charge of works to be executed at Three Rivers, if there is a harbour board there, and I think there is. There is a harbour board at Quebec, and therefore within the jurisdiction of the Quebec Harbour Commissioners his department has charge of the public expenditure. But if wharfs are to be built between Quebec and Montreal outside the very limited jurisdiction of the harbour commissioners, they are not to be attributed to my hon. friend's department, but they fall under the Department of Public Works. Lighthouses to be constructed above Montreal-and there is no subject which it seems to me comes more properly under the jurisdiction of the Department of Marine and Fisheries-those lighthouses, so far as their construction is concerned, belong to the Department of Public Works. The canal navigation remains where it was under the control of the Department of Railways and Canals. All wharfs or improvements to be constructed above Montreal, although intimately connected with navigation, unless they are to be constructed within the jurisdiction of the harbour commissioners, are completely outside the attribution of the department of my hon. friend We are, I believe this year, to execute very important and commendable improvements at Port Colborne which are very important: to the inland navigation of this country. Unless there are harbour commissioners at Port Colborne, and I am not aware that there are any, all those improvements will be constructed outside the control of the department of my hon. friend. That is the way I understand it. I do not think there are as yet harbour commissioners appointed for the ports of Port Arthur and Fort William. Any improvements we make there in the way of construction work would therefore be under the Department of Public Works and not under the department of my hon. friend. In other words, there has been a creation to the department of my bon. friend, but it is limited as indicated in the Order in Council read by him.
What 1 would like to ask my hon. friend is this :	Upon what principle did the government proceed in that division, in that attribution to his department of works which previously were under the control of the Department of Public Works ? What was the guiding principle ? Was it, as everything leads us to believe, a mere compromise between my hon. friend and the head of the Department of Public Works by which the latter relinquished some of his patronage, if I may use such an expression, a certain part of the subject previously attributed to it, in order to satisfy my hon. friend ? Was it that, or

*was there some principle which guided the government in making that attribution ? Ol course once we depart from the principle that all works of construction performed by the government, in whatever department they may belong, belong of right to the Department of Public Works, the moment, 1 say, we depart from the principle as we have upon the present occasion I do not see why that department, which used to be the most important, should not gradually be shorn of all its attributes. In England undoubtedly, in France, I believe, and in the United States there is no Department of Fublie Works. In those countries I understand, the departments have to construct themselves the works that they need; there is no special department of state to which the work of public construction is confided as has been the case in this country since confederation. That is also, I think, the system adopted in several provinces of the Dominion. I say once we depart from that principle I see no reason in reality why each, department should not have charge of its own construction, and why the Department of Public Works snould not be replaced by some new department which might supply all the many wants of a rapidly growing country like our own. I would like to know from my hon. friend what is the principle which guided the government in the division of the public works, and the attribution to his own department of those specially indicated in the Order in Council ?

The Order in Council explains itself very well, and is easy to understand. The government of this country .thought proper to delegate to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries certain functions which before had been performed by the Minister of Public Works. These are duly set forth in the Order in Council. Take for instance, the business of hydrographic surveys, which constituted an extraordinary anomaly in the administration of that branch of the public service. Part of those surveys were made by the Department of Railways and Canals, a part by the Department of Public Works, and still another part by the Department of Marine and Fisheries,t although by statute constituting the Department of Marine and Fisheries, all the hydrographic surveys should have been conducted by it and were attributed to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The Order in Council has settled that point and this work is now entirely confided to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Certain works which belonged entirely, according to the opinion of the government, to the control and supervision of the Department of Public Works were attributed to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. These include the most important national works of this country, the ship channel between Montreal and Quebec, and the equipment of the St. Lawrence. The ship channel between Montreal and Quebec is an essential part of our national highway. It is a work of the greatest importance and there would be really no national highway if the ship channel between Montreal and Quebec were not equipped and put in such a condition as to offer all the security and facilities that the trade and commerce of this country require. If I understand well my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier he would have liked if the whole of the work connected with minor improvements upon the route of the St. Lawrence, the construction of wharfs on the River Richelieu or on Lake St. Louis in his own county or in remote places in Canada, had been confided to me. There are thousands of small wharfs, some of them important, which are not really connected with what is known as the national route of the St. Lawrence and which are not therefore confided to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. In our judgment we thought that everything that was constructed in the general sense of the word should remain properly under the control of the Department of Public Works. What is the difference after all ? I would have liked probably, if I had consulted my own ambition, that everything should have been placed under my control, but after considering my capacity and realizing my position I came to the conclusion that my department could not embrace the construction of all these different works. I ask what is the difference after all whether these wharfs are constructed by the Department of Public Works or by the Department of Marine and Fisheries because after being constructed they are handed over to the Department of Marine and Fisheries to look after and administer. It makes no difference after-all. It does not make very much difference whether the Department of Marine and Fisheries or the Department of Public Works controls the expenditure of the money. There is a higher and more important question than that. My hon. friend seems to be under a misapprehension when he says that the wharfs and piers remain under the control of the Department of Public Works. That is not the case according to the law. The law provides that after these wharfs and piers are constructed they shall be handed over to the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to administer. My hon. friend is also under a misapprehension about the construction of lighthouses. The construction of lighthouses, the establishment of aids to navigation, and the furnishing of whatever is necessary for the safe navigation of the St. Lawrence route have been since 1872 under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries and they continue to be under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
Does my hon. friend say that the construction of lighthouses belongs to his department ?
And all were satisfied to administer the department as they found it.

Well, of course every one has his own tastes. I do not reproach them for not having thought well to improve the national route of the St. Lawrence, but I will point out that this government has taken the matter in hand, and it is going to show the people of Canada and the people of the United States, as well, that the St. Lawrence route is the great national highway for this part of the North American continent, and that it can compete with any other route in the United States. As I said, I do [DOT] not reproach the Conservative Ministers of Marine and Fisheries for not having dealt with the St. Lawrence route, but I point out to the people of Canada that the improvements are now going on. and I do not think they will bo disposed to blame the government for having made certain departmental changes. The question for us to consider is : is this work well carried on ; are the plans well matured ; is the execution of the work in the best interests of the country ? If these questions can be answered in the affirmative, then the people of Canada will take very little stock in minor considerations as to what minister is in charge of the execution of the policy of the government in this regard. My hon. friend seems much concerned that I have not the administration of the canals. Well, I am a new minister and have quite a good deal to look after now. and I am not ashamed to confess, a good deal to learn. I do not pretend to be perfect, but at the same time I am doing my best to administer the affairs which I have under my control at the present time. I may say that I am perhaps not as well posted as I would like to be in the fishery branch of my department, because I have not had the advantage of visiting the different parts of the Dominion to ascertain for myself the requirements of the people. I can say, however, without fear of contradiction, that as regards the port of Montreal and the channel between Montreal and Quebec, I have some knowledge of the needs of the situation, and I trust I may be able to apply that knowledge to the best advantage of the people of Canada. As to the lighting of the Sf. Lawrence route, we are trying to do the best we can. We are adopting the most modern apparatus so that we may give satisfaction, not only to the shipping trade entering Montreal from the east, but also to the transportation business coming to that port from the west. I think our efforts are directed in the proper way. If my hon. friend is not satisfied with what has been done, I must tell him I am perfectly satisfied. My friends are perfectly satisfied also and he is welcome as he was in 1902 in my division of Maisonneuve, to come and preach the same doctrine as he has preached tonight. I am perfectly willing to have my friends judge me by my acts and what I am doing.

My hon. friend has display ed a great deal of irritation unnecessarily. I do not know that there is any electricity in the atmosphere that would contribute to irritate my hon. friend, but he has given us a political harangue unnecessarily and has refrained from answering a very plain question. What I asked my hon. friend was this : There has been a redistribution of the work of the departments. I mildly, gently, mellifluously asked what principle had guided the government in that work of division, and the minister gets up and says he has made great improvements in the St. Lawrence, that this government is responsible for those improvements, and that people threw insults at him in his election. 1 never did anything of that kind myself, and I do not know that anybody else did. I never met my hon. friend during tliat election. I thought we had a right in that election to say that the 'Department of Public Works had been, in our opinion, unnecessarily taken from our province. We may have been wrong, but I think that was a legitimate question to discuss, and my hon. friend thought it so important that he said that the department of which he was taking charge was to be a new department altogether, and that everything that concerned navigation throughout the country, to use his own words, from the extreme west to the east, from the coast of the Pa oific down to Nova Scotia, on the coast of the Atlantic, any construction work with reference to piers, lighthouses, or any work of construction in connection with navigation, which belong to the Department of Public Works, would be transferred to him. He was elected upon that new programme which he defined in that election. I stated a moment ago that the system which has prevailed in Canada has been that all con struction of this and every kind whatever, for post offices, for military use, for any

department, was performed in this country by the Department of Public Works. In England, where there are forty-five minis ters, every minister controls the construction work of his own department. We have a different principle. My hon. friend preached through his election that that principle was going to be changed. He has changed it in part. He has taken a part out of the Public Works Department. A man cannot get up in this House and ask my hon. friend the principle and the line of conduct laid down in that division without getting from him a refusal to answer and an appeal to popular passion. I find that strange, and I repeat that I am sorry the minister refused to explain to me and to this committee why it is that if a wharf is to be built at St. Lambert, opposite Montreal, he has nothing to do with that construction, and if it is to be built at Hochelaga, within the limits of the jurisdiction of the harbour commissioners, it beiongs to him entirely. My hon. friend will not answer that question, and I will let it rest there. This is a very important item, and I wish to ask my hon. friend to give the committee a general idea as to how he proposes to spend this large sum. What are specifically the improvements that are going to be carried out this year in that ship channel, which interests the business and trading community of this country in such a large degree ? There is a very good report by Mr. Lafleur, acting Chief Engineer of the Department of Public Works, in the report of the Minister of Public Works last year, which gives a great deal of information. X find, amongst other things, not quite a justification of the proud boast which is made by the minister that he had inaugurated, and his government had carried out, under him, very important, improvements. I find that what has been done for the past ten years in the ship channel is but the carrying out of a plan laid down in 1844, I think before my hon. friend was born, certainly before I was born. We are carrying out that programme of deepening and improving the channel between Quebec and Montreal, and no doubt my hon. friend will contribute his part, as other ministers have done, to the carrying out of that plan first enunciated by the Hon. John Young, and which we have been carrying out ever since. The channel between Montreal and Quebec is 160 miles long. Sixty-five per cent of that channel requires no improvements, it is deep enough and wide enough to admit of the passage of vessels. The only improvement to be made there is the proper lighting of the channel. I find in Mr. Lafleur's report that the plan is to give the channel a depth of 30 feet from Montreal to Quebec, a width of at least 450 feet, which is the least that is safe, and where there are curves a width of at least 050 or 700 feet, or even more. No doubt it would be desirable that that channel should be wider, a depth of 30 feet and a width of 450 feet is barely enough, and the object we Mr. MONK.
have in view is to give it a width which would avoid some of the accidents that have occurred and which have damaged the reputation of the channel. We have excavated over 36,000,000 cubic yards. We have expended for plant, shops, surveys, Ac., $2,331,527.23, and we have expended for dredging $4,910,155.62. We have seven dredges. My hon. friend told the committee before six o'clock that we are going to have an eighth dredge. I would like to know whether it is contemplated continuing the work of improvement during the present season, what parts of the channel he is going to dredge, and what other improvements he is going to make, besides dredging, in the way of lighting, and generally in the way of carrying out the suggestions so ably made to the government two years ago by the shipping interests of Montreal, who carried on an Investigation at their own expense and laid the result of that investigation before the government, from whom they obtained the promise that their suggestions would be carried out. Where are we going to increase the depth and the width of the channel, and what improvements are we going to carry out in the way of lighting the channel ? Are any new buoys going to be added in order to secure safe navigation ? Can any hon. friend give us any valid reason for the unfortunate number of accidents which have occurred in that channel sincj the beginning of the season ? I find in Mr. Lafleur's report that last year we had eight accidents in the River St. Lawrence. The accidents which have occurred this year appear to be due in a large proportion to negligence on the part of somebody ; but whatever may be the cause, they have inflicted serious injury on our channel and make people skeptical as regards the accomplishment of the very excellent object which my hon. friend has in view, namely, of having the navigation of the St. Lawrence just as safe and free from risk as is the ocean navigation to the great American ports. My hon. friend has stated that under his administration, and that of the past few years, the insurance rates have greatly diminished. Is that the case, and what is the-diminution ?
My hon. friend is mistaken. What I said was that we had in sight the diminution of the rates ef insurance.

Then I misunderstood my hon. friend. But as I understand it-and I see my hon. friend from St. Lawrence division (Mr. Bickerdike) is in his seat, who is conversant with this subject-we are handicapped in the way of rates. The St. Lawrence route is mulcted in heavier rates than the American ports. That is a very serious disability for which I am told is no cause. There is no reason for it except the ipse dixit of the English underwriters, and it is most desirable that that

inequality should disappear. My hon. friend has a large sum at his disposal. He contemplates important improvements, and he states to the committee that he is certain that after those improvements have been carried out, the disability I refer to will either disappear or be seriously diminished. What guarantee can my hon. friend offer as to that V 1 would be prepared to vote an additional sum if my hon. friend can state to this committee, that he has conferred with the underwriters and that the improvements he contemplates will result in a removal of. that grave disability from which we suffer of being burdened with heavier rates of insurance than the American ports. Since my hon. friend, in a moment of irritation, which I cannot very well explain, has judged fit not to answer my hrst question, this one I beg him to believe is in no way connected with politics. The ship channel is to me a question apart from politics. It is a business matter which interests the whole Dominion and the city of Montreal in particular, and if my hon. friend will give me a little enlightenment on the points I have mentioned, I shall be very much obliged to him.

My hon. friend is under a misapprehension. Because 1 thought proper to explain as clearly as my control of the English language would permit, a few of the points which he thought proper to charge against the government, he feels that there was electricity in the air. My hon. friend may have felt it, but I did not and there was no cause for it. Now he says that the plan we are executing is one which was begun in 1844. Sir, the plan now being carried out was never begun in 1844. What was begun in 1844 was an attempt to dredge the channel through the Lake St. Peter flats, and whatever information the hon. gentleman has taken upon himself to give to the committee, he has taken from the reports of the Public Works Department for 1903 under the heading ' History of the ship channel.'
The actual improvements were commenced in 1844, and continued by the government as a public work until 1846, and abandoned the following year owing to opposition to the location of the channel.
Legislation was passed in 1850 transferring the plant and authorizing the Montreal Harbour Commissioners to borrow money and proceed with the works as they should deem bestk
From 1851 to 1888 all operations for the improvement of the St. Lawrence between Montreal and Quebec were carried on by the Montreal Harbour Commissioners, the interest on the cost of the work being defrayed by a tonnage tax on all vessels drawing 10 feet and upwards.
In 1888 the channel from Montreal to Cap h la Roche was completed to 27J feet at or-242
dinary low water, and from there to Quebec 27i feet at half tide. ,
The government decided in 1888 to re-adopt the River St. Lawrence ship channel as a public work.
Under the Public Works Department, from 1888 to 1898, the work begun by the Harbour Commissioners was continued.
The difficult rock work at Cap a. la Roche and Cap Charles was completed, as designed.
Almost all of the dredged portions of the river, except the channel in Lake St. Peter, were cleaned up or deepened, and many, curves and narrow places were widened.
Surveys were made, and between Cap Charles and Quebec, to avoid the necessity of waiting for the tide, channels were dredged, through several shoals.
The extraordinary low water * of 1895 and 1897, and the increase in the size of vessels* urgently called for a wider and deeper channel. '
In 1897 it was decided to construct new plant consisting of large and powerful dredges, tugs, barges, &c., suitable for channel improvement on a large scale.
It was only in 1899 that the present plans were fairly started and the new plant acquired. My hon. friend asked me what was going to be done, and before six o'clock I gave him the details of what we expected to accomplish with this sum of $588,000. We propose to complete the channel as planned in 1899 and to make it a thirty feet channel the whole length between Montreal and Quebec and from 450 feet to '750 feet wide as required. From the report I have from the engineer in charge of the channel, I take the following :
In view of the improvements already com-, pleted, and those expected to be completed! in the near future, I have to-day forwarded to you a report recommending for the consideration of the lighthouse board, a number of improvements and additions to the lighting and buoy -service on the River St. Lawrence-ship channel, between Longue Pointe and Batiscan.
The list calls for some 20 new piers, most of them ice-breaking concrete structures, 27 new lighthouses, and some 12 to 15 gas buoys.
These piers and permanent lights will be necessary in view of the proposal to prolong, navigation in the autumn and spring, and toi operate ice-breaking steamers.
During these operations buoys will not be available, and shore marks must be relied upon exclusively. The number and character of the lights therein suggested, would give a system of lighting equal in type and protection to the [DOT] general design of the improved thirty foot channel which is being dredged. With the exception of the widening in Lake St. Peter the dredging throughout the three divisions will be completed some time in 1905. The depth will also be completed in Lake St. Peter with the bends all enlarged, so that between Batiscan anchorage and Longue Pointe, the eastern limit of Montreal harbour, thirty foot navigation will be available at extreme low water. From Batiscan anchorage to Quebec, by taking advantage of the tide, vessels of the same draught may pass. The lighting from Quebec up to Batiscan is for the present channel about sufficient, as it is



.not advised that deep draught vessels should pass Cap a la Roche at night. The completion [DOT]of the improvement by dredging and the placing of the lights as suggested will mark a further important step in the perfecting of navigation iby the St. Lawrence route.
With the details that I gave before six o'clock I think there is sufficient information to enable the committee to form the opinion that the work which is proposed to be carried out under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries is purely and simply the execution of the plan which was adopted in 1899 and the carrying out of a system of lighting in such a perfect manner [DOT]that the navigation between Montreal and Quebec will be made just as safe as it is in the best waters in the world. But, the department does not intend to stop there There are other improvements as regards aids to navigation in the Lower St. Lawrence which are being considered by the department, and as this work is in the same hands I think it will help in having it executed more rapidly and in a better condition than it was carried on before.

I do not know whether the hon. gentleman was affecting indignation or not when he made a rather heated reply to my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). The hon. gentleman sat down without giving a single reason why a portion of the Department of Public Works and a small portion of the Department of Railways and Canals should have been taken away from these departments or why he should have attempted, merely upon an election pledge, to dismantle other departments. I would like to ask him if it means a vote of want of confidence in the gentleman who presided over the Department of Public Works. Does the hon. gentleman mean to say by his action that the present hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sutherland) was unable to perform the duties which were assigned to him ? Was that the reason or was it because the hon. gentleman wanted more patronage ? The hon. gentleman did not take the pains to tell the committee. He tells the committee very frankly that he has much to learn in respect to his own department. I am pretty well persuaded that this committee will conclude that the first thing that the hon. gentleman ought to do Is to master every detail in his own department before he undertakes work belonging to other departments. He is a new minister, he has only been a short time in his department and yet after entering it, in fact before he had been fairly seated in his department, the first thing he did when he went to his constituents was to make the promise that he would make a raid upon other departments. I was expecting the hon member for London (Mr. Hyman) to pronounce a eulogium upon the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries for his having pirated largely other departments and taken over other work. Was it Mr. PREFONTAINE.
essential to his election that he should have made a pledge in the city of Montreal that he would take over portions of other departments ? That was a part of the hon. gentleman's election pledge and he has been strong enough to redeem it. He has been strong enough to take other men _ by the throat, men who have retired from this House in consequence of it, men who are to-day absent from the House largely on the ground that the hon. genfleman took a portion of other departments in fulfilment of an election pledge and he is now pluming himself upon what he has done. I will leave it to the country to judge whether the hon. gentleman is discharging these duties better than they were discharged before. I have very grave doubts as to that part of it. I do not believe he is doing so. I believe they were as well discharged before as the hon. gentleman discharges them, and the country will expect some explanation from the hon. gentleman as well as from the right hon. Prime Minister as to the reasons why the hon. gentleman took from the Department of Public Works portions that could have been as well administered under the old order of things. There was no pretence that they could not have been and this change was only made to satisfy the greed of the hon. gentleman and to give him greater power.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
On this side of the House I do not think there sits an hon. gentleman who is not quite willing to vote $588,000 or any other sum which may be required for the purpose of improving the national highway, but I would like to inquire from the hon. gentleman why the money is frittered away as it is. 1 find in the Auditor General's Report of last year that large sums of money were expended upon articles that have nothing to do with aids to navigation. I find at page Y-30 that $719.50 was paid to Wm. Robertson & Son, Halifax and charged to the ship channel and I want the hon. minister to explain what these expenditures have to do with the improvement of the ship channel. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: My hon. friend need not criticise the member for Leeds as not being willing to spend money to give the Duke of York or any other" notable person from England, or elsewhere, a fitting reception. speechtext: I do not think the Duke of York ever went aboard one of the dredges.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Last year we asked for an appropriation of $400,000, but we find it was not possible to complete the year for that sum, and we ask for a further sum of $40,000 to complete the service' of the year which has just lapsed. speechtext:

Northwest Mounted Police-to provide for gratuity and pension to the widow and children of the late Arthur Frederick Montford Brooke, staff-sergeant in the Northwest Mounted Police, who was drowned while on duty, $1,204.25.
'Sir WILFRID LAURIER. Sergeant Brooke was drowned in crossing a river while on duty. I think he was out arresting a prisoner. There had been a freshet, which washed away the ford, and as a consequence the horses lost their footing and Sergeant Brooke was drowned. We give his family the same gratuity that we would have given if he had been killed in action. In 1885, we gave a pension to the families of those mounted policemen who had been killed in action, and this is calculated in exactly the same way, according to rules which have been in force for many years.
Northwest Mounted Police-to provide for a gratuity for the widow of the late J. A.. Beauprd, interpreter in the Northwest Mounted Police, who was drowned while on duty, $420.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Beaupre was an interpreter who accompanied Sergeant Brooke on that occasion. He did not belong to the regular staff of the mounted police, but was employed from time to time, as occasion required; and we give his widow the sum that we have been giving others under similar circumstances.

I have no objection to this item. As a rule these are poor men, and I think that something should be done for the families of those who lose their lives in the employment of the government. I am sorry the government draws the line so close.

Only a short time before he left the department he discussed the matter with me, and I hope that before very long some action will be taken.

We have had that hope expressed every year for the last three or four years. We are living in hope and likely to die in despair if no greater effort be made than has been made hitherto. speechtext: This is a case in which the government and the company who own the harbour propose to co-operate in making the repairs. The plan proposed is that the company should undertake to perform the work and make this a public harbour, with a schedule of wharfage rates to be approved by the government. Many years ago this was quite a shipping point, but when the small mines became amalgamated with the large mines in Cape Breton, the company ceased shipping coal in Glace Bay. Since that time a large settlement, running into 20,000 people, has grown up within a radius of two or three miles, and the people are very anxious that the harbour should be opened and utilized for the shipping of coal and also for the bringing in of produce by vessel from different parts of the Dominion.

I visited the locality since last session and saw the harbour. It is an artificial harbour and the ownership of the land is vested in a company. No doubt the work is very desirable, as there is a large community there and a great deal of business is done. We see rows of houses where only a few years ago there was a forest. The community is not only large but rapidly increasing and very progressive. The difficulty last year was as to the status of the harbour after the money of the country would be expended on it. The government were not able to state exactly what the arrangement would be in that regard, but it was the view of the Finance Minister that the harbour should be public so that all vessels would have the same right of entry Mr. HYMAN.
as if it had been a natural harbour in the first instance instead of an artificial one, subject of course to the rights of private property in the wharfs or docks which might be constructed by private enterprise. Not only is the company interested, which proposes to bear part of the expense, but the people of the community are interested in giving to this harbour the status of public navigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The company have not been seeking this change at all.
